n: Argentina — junta's 'systematic plan' to appropriate babies (2012 verdict)
place: Buenos Aires (ESMA naval school and other clandestine detention centres)
who: Argentine military junta; armed forces and security forces; ESMA
cover: Children's original identities were hidden and they were registered as the biological children of military families and regime allies.
d: On 5 July 2012 Federal Oral Criminal Tribunal No. 6 of Buenos Aires found that the military junta had run a systematic plan to abduct children born to detained or disappeared mothers, between 1976 and 1983. Former dictator Jorge Videla was sentenced to 50 years and the last dictator, Reynaldo Bignone, to 15 years; nine other defendants received 15 to 40 years (MercoPress). The trial covered about 31–35 abductions. The tribunal convicted Bignone of crimes against humanity for implementing the plan.

n: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
d: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

n: Vietnam — Nam Dinh ring: 266 babies sold for foreign adoption
who: Heads of two provincial social welfare centres; doctors and nurses at village clinics
d: In September 2009 a court in Nam Dinh tried 16 people, including the head of two social welfare centres and village clinic doctors and nurses, for 'abuse of power and authority'. They allegedly solicited infants from poor families and falsified documents saying the babies were abandoned; 266 babies were sent for foreign adoption from 2005 to July 2008. In April 2008 the US embassy in Hanoi had reported desertion numbers rising 17-fold or more at orphanages in 7 provinces, and Vietnam did not renew its adoption agreement with the US when it expired in September 2008.

n: Marshall Islands — Paul Petersen 'baby mill' adoption scheme
who: Paul Petersen, Maricopa County (Arizona) Assessor and adoption lawyer
d: Petersen, an elected Arizona official, paid recruiters to bring pregnant Marshallese women to the US, paying them about $10,000 to give up their babies and charging adoptive couples about $35,000, although the Compact of Free Association bars Marshallese travel to the US for adoption. Charged in October 2019 in Utah, Arizona and Arkansas, he pleaded guilty in all three courts in June 2020 (human smuggling, fraud, communication fraud) and was sentenced in December 2020 in federal court in Arkansas to more than six years in prison. He also fraudulently obtained about $814,000 in Arizona Medicaid funds for the women.

n: India — Andhra Pradesh adoption racket (Tender Loving Care Home)
who: St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home and other agencies
d: On 22 March 2001 Hyderabad police arrested a man carrying three baby girls allegedly bound for St Teresa's Tender Loving Care Home; other agencies were also flagged. A chargesheet said the home earned Rs 3.33 crore from intercountry adoptions, mainly to the US, in 1999–2001. On 31 August 2005 Sister Teresa Maria Kattikaran and nine others were sentenced to six months' imprisonment for cheating and forgery, and Andhra Pradesh became the first state to bar private agencies from placing children.

n: United States — Georgia Tann / Tennessee Children's Home Society black-market adoptions
who: Tennessee Children's Home Society (Shelby County branch) under Georgia Tann
d: From 1924 to 1950 Georgia Tann used the Memphis branch of the Tennessee Children's Home Society to take children from poor families and sell them, charging up to $5,000 for out-of-state adoptions when Tennessee adoptions cost about $7. A state investigation into adoption fraud led to the home's closure in 1950; Tann died before its findings were published.

n: Ethiopia — adoption abuses; Ethiopia bans foreign adoption (2018)
who: Orphanages and foreign adoption agencies operating in Ethiopia
d: Adoptions abroad grew from 262 in 2002 to more than 3,887 in 2008; Canadian families reported orphan papers for children whose parents were alive, and the US State Department found Better Futures Adoption Services involved in child trafficking, which lost its licence in February 2011. Ireland (October 2007), Australia (December 2009) and Denmark (March 2016) suspended adoptions from Ethiopia. Parliament banned adoption by foreigners in January 2018, effective 18 February 2018, citing abuse and neglect abroad after a US couple's 2013 conviction over the death of an adopted Ethiopian girl.

n: Spain — children of Republican prisoners taken by the Franco regime
place: Women's prisons and Auxilio Social homes across Spain
who: Franco regime; Auxilio Social; Women's Protection Board (Patronato de Protección a la Mujer); Falange
cover: Names were changed so children could be given to pro-regime families; the 1977 Amnesty Law has hindered investigation, and many Women's Protection Board files went missing in 1996.
d: A 1940 law allowed imprisoned mothers to keep children only until age three, after which the state took custody; 12,043 Republican children were in state custody in 1943. In 2008 Judge Baltasar Garzón characterised the removals as crimes against humanity and said the Falange was involved in kidnapping or forcibly repatriating children and changing their names. In January 2011 families of 261 babies who disappeared from hospitals over about fifty years took their cases to the attorney general; lawyers' estimates of up to 300,000 were rejected by a 2026 forensic study, which did not dispute about 30,000 children placed in state care.

n: Indonesia — baby trafficking syndicate selling infants to Singapore
place: Pontianak (West Kalimantan) and Tangerang; babies from West Java
who: Syndicate of recruiters, caretakers and document forgers
d: In July 2025 West Java police said a syndicate had sold at least 25 babies since 2023, mostly to buyers in Singapore, some 'reserved while still in the womb', for 11–16 million rupiah each, after preparing fraudulent family cards and passports in Pontianak. Thirteen people were arrested and six babies about to be trafficked were rescued; police sought Interpol help to trace the adopters.

n: France — state report finds 'illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption
who: French government and adoption associations
cover: The report said public authorities were alerted early, including at the highest levels, and were late in taking action.
d: In March 2024 France released an assessment acknowledging that its government had long known of 'the existence of illicit practices of a systemic nature' in intercountry adoption, and that diplomatic and association archives showed these practices existed in countries over long periods. France received 11,165 Korean children 1968–2008 among others.

n: Sierra Leone — 29 Makeni children sent to US adopters without parents' consent (HANCI)
who: Help A Needy Child International (HANCI)
d: In 1998 about 29 children at HANCI's centre in Makeni were taken to Freetown for medical checks and never returned; parents later learned they had been adopted by Americans. Sierra Leone suspended adoptions on 21 May 2009. In April 2012 a presidential commission shut HANCI down and concluded the biological families 'cannot be said to have genuinely consented'.

n: Haiti — 2007: children trafficked for international adoption returned to parents
who: A Haitian centre holding children awaiting international adoption
d: In 2007 a Haitian centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting international adoption to their families, after misleading parents with payments and holding the children in 'inhumane conditions' for months or years, according to the International Organization for Migration. An October 2007 report said officials had returned 50 trafficked children with 100 more awaiting rescue.

n: Kincora Boys' Home, Belfast — Hart Inquiry findings
place: Kincora Boys' Home, east Belfast, Northern Ireland
who: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast Welfare Authority / Eastern Health and Social Services Board); RUC investigations; MI5
cover: Hart found MI5 'consistently obstructed a proper line of inquiry' during the 1980s RUC Caskey Phase Three investigation, and found numerous missed opportunities to detect and stop the abuse.
d: The Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart reported on 20 January 2017. It confirmed that 38 boys at Kincora were sexually abused; three staff members, Joseph Mains, Raymond Semple and William McGrath, were convicted. Hart found that Kincora was not a homosexual brothel, that no security agency used it to entrap or blackmail men, and that there was 'no credible evidence' that prominent people such as civil servants, businessmen or Sir Maurice Oldfield were involved; he called the honey-trap claims 'unfounded myths'. He did criticise MI5 for obstructing the 1980s police investigation. Some former residents rejected the conclusions.

n: Nottinghamshire and Nottingham councils (incl. Beechwood) — IICSA
place: Nottingham and Nottinghamshire (Beechwood Children's Home, Mapperley)
who: Nottinghamshire County Council and Nottingham City Council residential and foster care; Beechwood Children's Home
cover: Only two disciplinary actions, both inadequate, followed the many allegations at Beechwood; known perpetrators were allowed to continue fostering and abused again.
d: IICSA reported on 31 July 2019 that sexual abuse was widespread in the two councils' residential and foster care in the 1970s–1990s. About 350 people reported abuse. From the late 1970s to 2019, 16 residential staff and 10 foster carers were convicted of sexually abusing children in their care, plus 12 convictions for harmful sexual behaviour by children against other children. The inquiry concluded that 'neither of the Councils learned from their mistakes'.

n: Quarriers, Aberlour and Barnardo's homes — Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry
place: Scotland (Quarriers Village, Bridge of Weir, and other homes)
who: Quarriers, Aberlour Child Care Trust and Barnardo's residential homes in Scotland
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's third case study findings, published 7 January 2020, concluded that children in residential care run by Quarriers, Aberlour and Barnardo's between 1921 and 1991 suffered physical, emotional and sexual abuse. These voluntary providers cared for children placed by local authorities across Scotland.

n: Odenwaldschule, Heppenheim — abuse by headmaster Gerold Becker and teachers
who: Odenwaldschule (private, state-recognised progressive boarding school); headmaster Gerold Becker, music teacher Wolfgang Held
cover: After victims came forward in 1998 and the Frankfurter Rundschau reported it in November 1999, a promised review did not take place; prosecutors in Darmstadt dropped the case under the statute of limitations. Becker died in 2010 without facing legal consequences.
d: Lawyers Claudia Burgsmüller and Brigitte Tilmann, a former judge, were called in by the school to investigate; their 2010 report identified more than a dozen perpetrators, with former headmaster Gerold Becker and a music teacher named as the main abusers from the late 1960s, and 17 witnesses testifying against Becker. Later counts put the victims at at least 132 pupils abused by teachers between the 1960s and 1990s; the victims' association says at least 20 teachers were responsible. The abuse, long covered up, became widely public in 2010; pupil numbers and funding fell and in April 2015 the school's sponsoring association announced its closure. Becker also appears in the Hildesheim research as a figure in the Kentler network.

n: Samson Commission — sexual abuse of children in Dutch state care
who: Dutch children's homes and foster care (Jeugdzorg)
d: The commission chaired by former procurator-general Rieke Samson reported in October 2012 on sexual abuse of children in state-arranged care since 1945. It received 800 claims, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. It found the government, care homes and foster care services did not do enough to protect children and, once aware, lacked professionalism and courage to act.

n: Swedish inquiry into abuse in children's homes and foster care (Vanvårdsutredningen)
who: Swedish municipal children's homes and foster care
d: The government inquiry into abuse and neglect in Swedish children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980 reported in February 2011, recommending a public apology and SEK 250,000 for each person who suffered serious abuse; the apology ceremony was held at Stockholm City Hall in 2011. A compensation board set up on 1 January 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015 and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

n: Notre-Dame de Bétharram school — National Assembly commission of inquiry
who: Notre-Dame de Bétharram, a Catholic private school under contract with the state; Ministry of Education inspection
cover: The commission wrote that 'in the absence of action from a minister who was informed and in a position to intervene', abuse continued for years; it found state inspection of private schools under contract was weak and sanctioned teachers could move between schools undetected.
d: Priests, teachers and staff are accused of sexual and physical abuse of pupils from 1957 to 2004, with about 200 complaints filed in 2025. The National Assembly commission of inquiry (rapporteurs Violette Spillebout and Paul Vannier) published its report on 2 July 2025 with 50 recommendations, including rebuilding state inspections. It did not directly implicate François Bayrou, who said he had not grasped the seriousness of information he received; Vannier separately accused him of misleading parliament.

n: Cornwall Public Inquiry — institutional responses to historical abuse
who: Cornwall Community Police Service, Ontario Provincial Police (Project Truth), local probation office, Roman Catholic Diocese of Alexandria-Cornwall
cover: Commissioner Glaude found the Diocese's $32,000 settlement with complainant David Silmser contained an illegal clause, and called Cornwall police's investigation of his complaint 'deeply flawed', though he found no conspiracy between police and diocese.
d: The Cornwall Public Inquiry under Commissioner G. Normand Glaude reported in December 2009 at a cost of over $50 million. It found systemic failures by police, probation and the Catholic diocese in responding to historical sexual abuse allegations against adults in positions of trust in Cornwall. On the long-rumoured paedophile 'clan', Glaude made no finding, saying no investigation had provided conclusive evidence.

n: Los Angeles County juvenile halls and MacLaren Children's Center — $4bn settlement
place: Los Angeles County, California (MacLaren Children's Center, El Monte, and juvenile halls)
who: Los Angeles County Probation Department juvenile facilities; MacLaren Children's Center (closed 2003); county foster care
d: On 29 April 2025 the Los Angeles County Board of Supervisors unanimously approved a $4 billion settlement of more than 6,800 claims of sexual abuse, mostly in Probation Department juvenile facilities and at the MacLaren Children's Center in El Monte, plus foster care, dating back to the 1980s. It was the costliest such payout in county history.

n: 'Troubled teen' residential programmes — GAO 2007 investigation
who: Private residential treatment programmes, boot camps and wilderness programmes for youth
d: In testimony to Congress on 10 October 2007 (GAO-08-146T), the Government Accountability Office reported it had found thousands of allegations of abuse, some involving death, at residential treatment programmes for troubled youth, reviewing closed cases back to 1990. GAO did not verify each allegation.

n: Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse — final report
who: Religious, government and other institutions; evidence related to 3,489 institutions
cover: Case studies documented destroyed or unkept records and the protection of institutional reputation over children, e.g. the Catholic Diocese of Ballarat ('records were deliberately not made or kept or were destroyed').
d: The Royal Commission, announced in November 2012, delivered its final report on 15 December 2017 with a total of 409 recommendations across its reports. It held 8,013 private sessions, received 1,344 written accounts and heard evidence relating to 3,489 institutions. 58.1% of survivors in private sessions reported abuse in a religious institution, 32.5% in a government-run institution and 10.5% in other non-government institutions. The average age at first abuse was 10.4 years. Its recommendations led to the National Redress Scheme, which began on 1 July 2018.

n: Mullighan Inquiry — Children in State Care, South Australia
who: South Australian state guardianship system (Families SA and predecessors)
d: Commissioner Ted Mullighan's inquiry began in November 2004 and was widened in 2007 to children on the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara (APY) Lands. Its March 2008 report found 'that in the past 65 years the State has failed to protect some of the children in its care from sexual abuse' and that record-keeping on 924 children who died in state care was manifestly inadequate. It made 54 recommendations, and 400 suspected abusers were reported to South Australia Police.

n: Muzaffarpur shelter home — TISS audit and convictions
who: Sewa Sankalp Evam Vikas Samiti (state-funded NGO run by Brajesh Thakur); Bihar Social Welfare Department
cover: The then district child protection officer was among the accused; Bihar Social Welfare Minister Manju Verma resigned over the case; the Supreme Court criticised the state for funding the NGO and moved the trial to Delhi. CBI cleared Verma and her husband, a finding disputed by The Caravan.
d: A social audit of Bihar shelter homes by the Tata Institute of Social Sciences, submitted in April 2018, flagged sexual abuse at the Muzaffarpur girls' home run by Brajesh Thakur's NGO; an FIR followed on 31 May 2018. Medical examination indicated sexual abuse of 34 girls, most of them children. The Supreme Court took up the case and, at the CBI's request, transferred the trial to a POCSO court at Saket, Delhi, because the accused were influential in Bihar. On 20 January 2020 that court convicted Thakur and 18 others; Thakur was sentenced to life imprisonment and has appealed.

n: Tasmanian Commission of Inquiry — Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital, schools and out-of-home care
place: Tasmania (Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Deloraine; Launceston General Hospital)
who: Tasmanian Government: Ashley Youth Detention Centre, Launceston General Hospital paediatric ward, public schools, Child Safety Services, Tasmania Police
cover: Launceston General Hospital failed to act on a 2011 or 2012 disclosure about nurse James Griffin, leaving children at risk for eight years; Tasmania Police failed to act on 'highly probative' evidence from the Australian Federal Police in 2015; the government had been on notice about unlawful isolation at Ashley since at least 2013.
d: The commission, called in 2020 after a podcast aired allegations against Launceston General Hospital paediatric nurse James Griffin (who died in 2019 after being charged with child sexual offences), released a 3,500-page final report in 2023 with 75 findings and 191 recommendations. It found the state's response to child sexual abuse since 2000 had too often been inadequate, sometimes to protect reputations. Children at Ashley Youth Detention Centre had experienced systematic harm and abuse for decades and sexual abuse remained a 'live and current' risk; the commission repeated its call for Ashley to close. Premier Jeremy Rockliff apologised in parliament.

n: SENAME — deaths and abuse in Chilean state child protection
place: Chile (incl. Centro Galvarino, Estación Central, Santiago)
who: Servicio Nacional de Menores (SENAME), Ministry of Justice, and accredited private residences
d: The death of an 11-year-old girl at SENAME's Galvarino centre in Santiago in April 2016 exposed conditions in the system; in October 2016 SENAME disclosed 1,313 deaths of people in its programmes between 2005 and mid-2016. In a report released on 30 July 2018 the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child found the Chilean state responsible for 'grave violations' of the Convention, including sexual abuse, torture and cruel treatment in SENAME residences over 40 years, overcrowding of up to 60% and 210 deaths in residences 2005–2016. A former national director was questioned as a suspect over children's deaths in 2018.

n: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
place: Kathmandu Valley (Bagmati Province); children from Karnali and other rural districts
who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
d: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).

n: Flanders — historical abuse in youth institutions and boarding schools, parliamentary apology
who: Flemish youth institutions, youth centres and boarding schools
d: After clergy abuse cases, further cases emerged of child abuse in Flemish institutions between 1930 and 1990. A working group of experts led by child psychiatrist Peter Adriaenssens, set up by Welfare Minister Jo Vandeurzen, produced two reports recognising the wide scope of abuse. On 23 April 2014 Flemish Parliament Speaker Jan Peumans formally apologised to victims of abuse in boarding schools and youth centres. A temporary recognition and mediation commission set up in 2014 was later made permanent; it received 121 reports in 2024.

n: Cambodia — orphanages buying children to attract donations
place: Cambodia (incl. Siem Reap and Phnom Penh)
who: Private residential care institutions ('orphanages') in Cambodia
cover: The report states 'endemic corruption aids and abets trafficking crimes'.
d: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states: 'Some Cambodian orphanages purchase local children from economically disadvantaged families and subject them to malnutrition and unclean living conditions in their facilities for the purpose of attracting and profiting from charitable donations; some of these children are at further risk of sex trafficking and domestic servitude as a result of poor government oversight of adoption processes.' The same report links orphanages and trafficking in Nepal, Nigeria, Haiti, Sri Lanka and Moldova.

n: Serbia — 'Torment not Treatment' investigation of institutions for children and adults with disabilities
place: Serbia (Kulina, Stamnica, Vršac and other institutions)
who: Serbian state institutions for people with mental disabilities
cover: In 2006 the director of one institution refused to let investigators see a locked area and asked them to leave; Serbian officials called the allegations 'dark propaganda'.
d: Mental Disability Rights International's four-year investigation, released on 14 November 2007, covered conditions affecting more than 17,000 people with disabilities in Serbian institutions. It found children and adults tied to beds or kept in cribs for years, filthy conditions, contagious disease and no oversight, treatment it said was 'tantamount to torture'. It warned of a danger of sexual exploitation: at Vršac men and women lived in mixed wards and staff said they made no effort to determine whether sex was consensual.

n: Japan — Yomiuri survey of sexual misconduct by staff in children's homes
who: Children's homes (児童養護施設) in Japan
d: A Yomiuri Shimbun survey published in December 2021 found that in the five years to fiscal 2020 at least 47 staff at children's homes across Japan were confirmed to have committed indecent acts against children in their care, and that 69 children were victims. Only a summary of the survey was accessible; the full article was withdrawn by the provider.

n: Apna Ghar shelter, Rohtak — CBI court convictions
who: Apna Ghar, a government-funded shelter run by Jaswanti Devi and relatives
d: The case began in 2012 when three girls escaped from the government-funded Apna Ghar shelter and told police residents were physically and sexually abused and used as bonded labour. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights raided it in May 2012; Haryana sealed it in June 2012 and the CBI charge-sheeted ten people in August 2012. On 18 April 2018 a special CBI court in Panchkula convicted nine, including of rape, abortion without consent, bonded labour and offences under the Immoral Traffic (Prevention) Act and Juvenile Justice Act; on 27 April 2018 Jaswanti Devi, her son-in-law and a driver were sentenced to life. A former child development project officer who oversaw the shelter was acquitted.

n: French Operation Sangaris soldiers — alleged abuse of children, Bangui
who: French army, Operation Sangaris (not under UN command)
cover: The internal UN report was not passed to French authorities by the UN; the UN official who passed it on (Anders Kompass) was suspended and resigned in 2016 in protest at impunity.
d: An internal UN document revealed by The Guardian in April 2015 recorded interviews with six boys aged 9 to 13 who said French soldiers of Operation Sangaris had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014 at the displaced persons' camp at Bangui's M'Poko airport, in exchange for food rations. The Paris prosecutor had opened a preliminary inquiry in July 2014; the investigation eventually covered accusations by fifteen children, most interviewed in Bangui in 2015 and 2016. In January 2018 French investigating judges dismissed the case (non-lieu) for lack of sufficient charges, citing inconsistencies in testimony; the prosecutor said 'it cannot be affirmed at the end of the investigation that no sexual abuse was committed'. No soldier was charged.

n: MINUSCA — all Gabonese units withdrawn after SEA allegations (2021)
who: Gabonese military contingent, MINUSCA
d: On 15 September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA (about 450 personnel) would be repatriated after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse; Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report links most multiple-victim MINUSCA allegations of 2021 to one troop-contributing country repatriated that September.

n: ONUMOZ Mozambique — soldiers recruited girls aged 12–18 into prostitution (Machel study)
who: UN Operation in Mozambique (ONUMOZ) soldiers
d: The UN study 'Impact of Armed Conflict on Children' led by Graça Machel (August 1996) found that after the 1992 peace treaty, ONUMOZ soldiers recruited girls aged 12 to 18 into prostitution. It also found that in 6 of 12 country studies on sexual exploitation of children in armed conflict, the arrival of peacekeeping troops was associated with a rapid rise in child prostitution.

n: Afghanistan — bacha bazi by Afghan forces; US troops told not to intervene; SIGAR 2017
who: Afghan National Defense and Security Forces and Afghan Local Police commanders; US military chain of command
cover: NYT (2015) reported US soldiers were instructed not to intervene, in some cases even on US bases; US law (Leahy) required cutting aid to offending units but SIGAR/NYT reported that never happened. Capt. Dan Quinn was relieved and Sgt 1st Class Charles Martland initially separated after beating an ALP commander who admitted chaining and raping a 12-year-old boy (2011).
d: In September 2015 The New York Times reported that US soldiers had been told to ignore sexual abuse of boys by Afghan allies, describing it as rampant; nearly 100 members of Congress then asked the Special Inspector General for Afghanistan Reconstruction (SIGAR) to investigate. SIGAR's report, sent to Congress in 2017 and made public on 23 January 2018, found that as of August 2016 the Pentagon was tracking 75 gross human rights violations by Afghan security forces from 2010 to 2016, at least seven of them child sexual assault, and said 'the full extent of child sexual assault committed by Afghan security forces may never be known'. The Pentagon used the 'notwithstanding' exception to the Leahy Law to keep supporting implicated units, including approving continued funding in December 2015 for 12 units implicated in 14 violations.

n: Ukraine — rape and sexual violence by Russian forces incl. children (UN Commission of Inquiry)
place: Kyiv, Kherson and other formerly occupied areas
who: Russian armed forces and authorities
d: The Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine found that Russian authorities committed the war crimes of rape and other sexual violence; cases it investigated included a 16-year-old girl, and in September 2022 it said it had documented children raped, tortured and unlawfully confined. Ukraine's official Children of War platform records 23 children sexually abused, according to the Office of the Prosecutor General.

n: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
place: Sinjar, Ninewa → Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush, Galaxy hall), Raqqa
who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
d: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria; thousands remain missing.

n: Nigeria — UN-verified abduction and forced marriage of children by JAS and ISWAP (2024)
who: Jama'atu Ahlis Sunna Lidda'Awati Wal-Jihad (JAS/Boko Haram), ISWAP, Bakura
d: The UN verified the abduction of 991 children (354 boys, 637 girls) in Nigeria in 2024 by JAS (690), ISWAP (294) and Bakura (7), most for recruitment and use. It also verified sexual violence, all involving forced marriage, against 419 children (7 boys, 412 girls) by JAS (304), ISWAP (114) and Bakura (1). In 2023 the UN had verified sexual violence against 366 children following abduction.

n: Haiti — armed gangs' sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024)
who: Viv Ansanm gang coalition (411 cases) and other armed gangs
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children (523 girls, 43 boys) in Haiti in 2024, 411 attributed to the Viv Ansanm coalition; cases involved rape (406) and gang rape (160). This was up from 41 girls verified in 2023. Viv Ansanm was listed in the Secretary-General's annex for rape and other sexual violence against children, recruitment, killing and maiming, and attacks on schools and hospitals.

n: Central African Republic — UN-verified sexual violence and abduction of children (2024)
who: CPC coalition (UPC, 3R, anti-balaka); national defence forces; Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe; RSF
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 114 girls in CAR in 2024: CPC armed groups 58, government and pro-government forces 35 (national defence forces 21, Wagner Ti Azande/Azande Ani Kpi Gbe 9), PRNC 11, Sudanese RSF 2. It verified the abduction of 141 children, most for recruitment and/or sexual violence. The Secretary-General said he was deeply concerned by rising violations by government and pro-government forces.

n: Niger — UN-verified abduction of children (2023–2024)
who: JAS, ISWAP, ISGS, unidentified perpetrators; Niger security forces (one case 2023)
d: The UN verified the abduction of 202 children (102 girls) in Niger in 2024 by unidentified perpetrators (163), JAS (35), ISWAP (2) and ISGS (2), and sexual violence against five girls. In 2023 it verified sexual violence against 8 girls, one by the Niger security forces.

n: Colombia — sexual violence against girls by ELN, FARC dissidents, Clan del Golfo (UN verified)
who: ELN, FARC-EP dissident groups, Clan del Golfo; Colombian armed forces (2 cases 2023)
d: The UN verified sexual violence against 33 girls in Colombia in 2024, by the ELN (12), FARC-EP dissident groups (12), Clan del Golfo (7) and unidentified perpetrators. In 2023 it verified 26 cases, including 2 by the Colombian armed forces.

n: Kincora Boys' Home (Belfast) — claims of MI5/army intelligence complicity
place: Kincora Boys' Home, Upper Newtownards Road, east Belfast
who: Kincora staff (William McGrath, Raymond Semple, Joseph Mains — convicted 1981); alleged: MI5, army intelligence, RUC Special Branch
cover: Abuse allegations reached the RUC by 1977 without prosecution until 1980; the Hart inquiry found a 'catalogue of failures' by police and authorities. Former army officers Colin Wallace and Brian Gemmell said in 2014 that superiors stopped them passing on or pursuing information.
d: Three Kincora staff were convicted in 1981 of systematic sexual abuse of boys in their care. For decades it was alleged that McGrath, leader of the loyalist group Tara, was an MI5 agent and that intelligence services protected a ring of prominent abusers to blackmail them. On 20 January 2017 the Historical Institutional Abuse Inquiry chaired by Sir Anthony Hart found 'no credible evidence' that others were involved or that 'the security agencies were complicit in any form of sexual abuse in Kincora for any purpose', and said the 'honey pot' blackmail claim was without foundation; it said the government's promise to hand over all files had been honoured. In June 2025 former resident Gary Hoy settled his civil claim against the PSNI and Home Secretary, which alleged McGrath was protected as an MI5 agent, on confidential terms with no admission of liability.

n: Al Hassan (Ansar Eddine, Timbuktu) — ICC: convicted of torture/persecution; acquitted of rape and sexual slavery
who: Ansar Eddine / AQIM Islamic police in Timbuktu
d: On 26 June 2024 the ICC convicted Al Hassan Ag Abdoul Aziz of crimes against humanity and war crimes including torture and persecution in Timbuktu, but acquitted him of the war crimes of rape and sexual slavery (charges that included forced marriages of women and girls). Recorded here as an acquittal on the sexual-violence counts only.

n: Epstein — Palm Beach police investigation and 2006 state charge
who: Jeffrey Epstein (financier)
cover: Police chief Michael Reiter said state prosecutors under State Attorney Barry Krischer grew dismissive about six months in; he asked Krischer to step aside. The July 2006 state grand jury returned only one felony solicitation-of-prostitution count. Reiter then referred the case to the FBI.
d: In March 2005 a woman told Palm Beach police her 14-year-old stepdaughter had been paid to give Epstein a massage at his mansion. A 13-month police investigation identified about 35 girls. In July 2006 a state grand jury returned a single count of felony solicitation of prostitution and Epstein was arrested on 23 July 2006. Reiter later called the outcome 'the worst failure of the criminal justice system' in modern times.

n: Jean-Luc Brunel — Paris investigation into rape of minors (died before trial)
who: Jean-Luc Brunel; MC2 Model Management (New York/Miami), Karin Models
d: Paris prosecutors opened an inquiry in August 2019 into sex trafficking and sexual-assault allegations linked to Epstein, focused on French victims and French suspects. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel, who co-founded Karin Models in 1977 and later founded MC2 Model Management in the US with funding from Epstein, was detained at Charles de Gaulle airport in December 2020 as he tried to board a flight to Senegal, and was placed under formal investigation on suspicion of rape of minors and trafficking of minors for sexual exploitation. He was found hanged in his cell at La Santé prison on 19 Feb 2022, having been held for over a year. He denied wrongdoing and was never tried.

n: Peter Mandelson — 2026 arrest on suspicion of misconduct in public office (Epstein files)
who: Peter Mandelson (former UK ambassador to the US, former cabinet minister)
d: Mandelson was dismissed as UK ambassador to the US in Sept 2025 after emails showed he kept up his friendship with Epstein after Epstein's 2008 conviction. After the January 2026 DOJ release suggested he passed sensitive government information to Epstein about 15 years earlier, he left the Labour Party and House of Lords and the Metropolitan Police arrested him on 23 Feb 2026 on suspicion of misconduct in public office. He faces no allegation of sexual misconduct; recorded here for the network's political reach, not as an abuse case.

n: Claims that Epstein was tied to intelligence services
who: Claims about US and Israeli intelligence (unproven)
d: In July 2019 journalist Vicky Ward (Daily Beast) reported that Alexander Acosta had told Trump transition interviewers he was told Epstein 'belonged to intelligence' and to leave it alone; the source was not named. In its November 2020 report, the Justice Department's Office of Professional Responsibility said Acosta told it 'the answer is no' when asked whether Epstein was an intelligence asset, and found 'no evidence suggesting that Epstein was such a cooperating witness or intelligence asset'. Other claims circulate, including that Ghislaine Maxwell's father Robert Maxwell worked for Israeli intelligence and about Epstein's business ties to former Israeli PM Ehud Barak, who denies wrongdoing. No official body has found that Epstein worked for any intelligence service.

n: Cyril Smith MP — Cambridge House and Knowl View, Rochdale
who: Cyril Smith (Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992); Lancashire Constabulary; Director of Public Prosecutions; Rochdale Council
cover: Police evidence presented in 1970 led to no action; the CPS said in 2012 that Smith should have been charged and that he had been given an assurance in 1970 he would not be prosecuted. Press allegations in 1979 (Rochdale Alternative Press, Private Eye) produced no prosecution. He was knighted in 1988 though Margaret Thatcher had been told of the allegations.
d: Cyril Smith, Liberal MP for Rochdale 1972–1992, was alleged by eight men to have indecently assaulted them as teenagers in about 1961–1966; six had lived at Cambridge House hostel, which he helped set up. The Director of Public Prosecutions advised against prosecution in 1970, and CPS reviews in 1998 and 1999 did not lead to charges. He died on 3 September 2010, never charged. On 27 November 2012 Greater Manchester Police said the boys had been victims of physical and sexual abuse by Smith, and the CPS said he should have been charged. The IICSA report on Cambridge House, Knowl View and Rochdale (April 2018) found no evidence of improper influence on the DPP but said valuable opportunities to prosecute were lost in 1998 and 1999, and that discussions before his 1988 knighthood showed 'considerable deference to power'; witnesses also told it Smith assaulted boys at Knowl View School.

n: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
d: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing thousands of child abuse images (about 4,000; jailed four months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002 amid sex-crime allegations. In March 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11; he spent about two and a half years in jail there. In February 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape, four indecent assaults and one count of sex with a girl under 13, against three girls in 1975–1980, and sentenced to 16 years. Released in February 2023, he was recalled to prison in March 2023 for breaching licence conditions.

n: Dutroux affair — kidnap, abuse and murder of girls; police and justice failures
who: Marc Dutroux, Michelle Martin, Michel Lelièvre; Belgian Gendarmerie and judicial police
cover: Dutroux was released early in 1992 from a 13.5-year sentence over prosecutor and psychiatrist objections. Police missed chances, including voices heard in his cellar and unreviewed videotapes; rivalry between Gendarmerie and judicial police hampered the hunt. Judge Connerotte was removed in Oct 1996 for attending a victims' fundraising dinner.
d: Dutroux, on parole for earlier rapes, kidnapped six girls aged 8 to 19 in 1995–96; he was found guilty of kidnapping and raping all six, killing two and causing the deaths of two others. He was arrested in August 1996, and in October 1996 hundreds of thousands of Belgians joined the White March in Brussels to protest police and judicial failures. A parliamentary inquiry chaired by Marc Verwilghen sharply criticised the police investigation. On 22 June 2004 Dutroux was sentenced to life; his ex-wife Michelle Martin got 30 years and Michel Lelièvre 25; businessman Michel Nihoul was acquitted of kidnapping and conspiracy but convicted of drug trafficking and other crimes (five years). Belgium later reorganised its police forces.

n: Joël Le Scouarnec — surgeon convicted for 299 victims
who: Joël Le Scouarnec (surgeon); hospitals and medical regulators
cover: The FBI traced his downloading of abuse images in 2004; his 2005 conviction (4 months suspended) brought no restriction on practice. Prosecutors did not alert medical authorities; the regional medical body found no breach in 2006; a 2007 warning to the health ministry brought no action; a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction.
d: Le Scouarnec, a surgeon in western France, was convicted in Saintes in December 2020 of raping and sexually assaulting four children, including two of his nieces (15 years). At his second trial in Vannes he admitted abusing all 299 victims, mostly hospital patients, many under anaesthesia or waking from surgery, between 1989 and 2014; more than 250 were under 15. On 28 May 2025 the court sentenced him to the maximum 20 years. He is not part of an elite network; included as a professional whose standing protected him (setting is debatable — could be moved to 'care').

n: Jean Succar Kuri — Cancún child sexual exploitation ring
who: Jean Succar Kuri (hotelier); associates named in Lydia Cacho's reporting
cover: See the related record on journalist Lydia Cacho's 2005 arrest arranged after her book exposed the ring.
d: Cancún hotel businessman Succar Kuri was detained in the United States (reported as Los Angeles/Arizona) in 2004 at the request of Mexico's federal prosecutors and Interpol, after complaints by several girls, and was later returned to Mexico. In 2011 a federal district court convicted him and sentenced him to 13 years; on appeal by both sides a Cancún appeals court raised the sentence to 112 years, which was upheld. In 2023 a federal circuit court annulled the 112-year sentence over procedural flaws and ordered a new ruling on sexual abuse and child pornography offences against seven minors, which reduced his term. He died in Cancún on 14 June 2024 while still serving his sentence. Journalist Lydia Cacho's book 'Los demonios del Edén' described him as the head of a child-exploitation network and linked him to Puebla businessman Kamel Nacif and Governor Mario Marín.

n: Jerry Sandusky — Penn State football and The Second Mile
who: Jerry Sandusky (assistant coach); Pennsylvania State University; The Second Mile charity
cover: A 1998 report to Penn State police was not prosecuted. In 2001 graduate assistant Mike McQueary reported seeing Sandusky with a boy in a shower; it went to Joe Paterno, athletic director Tim Curley and vice-president Gary Schultz. The Freeh report (July 2012) found Paterno, president Graham Spanier, Curley and Schultz concealed Sandusky's activities. Curley, Schultz and Spanier were convicted of child endangerment in 2017.
d: Sandusky, a former Penn State assistant football coach, was charged in Nov 2011 and convicted in June 2012 of 45 counts of sexual abuse involving 10 boys, some assaulted on the Penn State campus; in Oct 2012 he was sentenced to 30–60 years. He met boys through The Second Mile charity he founded in 1977. The Freeh report (July 2012), commissioned by the university, found the most senior Penn State leaders showed 'total disregard' for the victims' safety. The NCAA fined Penn State $60m.

n: Jared Fogle (Subway spokesman) — child abuse material and paid sex with minors
who: Jared Fogle; Russell Taylor (co-conspirator); Subway
cover: Allegations surfaced in 2007 but the FBI acted only in 2015. A franchisee says she told Subway in 2008 about Fogle's messages seeking sex with a minor; Subway says it has no record.
d: After his Indianapolis home was raided in July 2015 in a child abuse material investigation, Fogle pleaded guilty to receiving child abuse material and travelling to engage in illicit sexual conduct with a minor, and on 19 Nov 2015 was sentenced to 188 months (15 years 8 months). He had already paid $100,000 restitution to each of 14 victims ($1.4m); two were 16 and 17 when he travelled to have sex with them.

n: McMartin preschool trial — 'satanic abuse' panic ends in acquittals
who: McMartin Preschool (accused: Ray Buckey, Peggy McMartin Buckey)
d: Claims of abuse at the McMartin Pre-School in Manhattan Beach, California, began in autumn 1983 with one small boy's report and grew to include allegations of 'satanic-like ritual'; interview techniques were later widely criticised. In January 1990, after nearly three years of trial, Peggy McMartin Buckey was acquitted of all 12 counts and Ray Buckey of 40 counts, with the jury deadlocked on 13; a retrial of Ray Buckey on eight counts ended in a deadlocked jury in July 1990, and the prosecution was dropped. None of the seven people charged was convicted of anything. The case cost taxpayers about $14m. Included as the template for 'ritual abuse' claims.

n: Knox Grammar School — headmaster failed to report teachers' abuse
who: Knox Grammar School; Uniting Church
cover: The Royal Commission (Sept 2016) found headmaster Ian Paterson never reported a student's abuse allegation to police in about 30 years, despite a duty from 1988; he let accused teachers resign and gave some positive references, and withheld information from a police officer.
d: After abuse was reported to police in 2009, five former Knox Grammar teachers were convicted of child sexual offences against students. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse held Case Study 23 on the school in February–March 2015, examining its handling of concerns about teachers between 1970 and 2009, and heard from 12 former students. Its September 2016 report found that former headmaster Ian Paterson (1969–1998) deliberately covered up allegations, placing the school's reputation ahead of student welfare; he had told the commission he did not tell police what he knew about teachers who were later convicted.

n: Haitian Football Federation — Yves Jean-Bart banned by FIFA
who: Yves Jean-Bart (FHF president since 2000)
d: On 30 April 2020 The Guardian reported accusations that Jean-Bart, president of the Haitian Football Federation since 2000, coerced young female players at the national training centre in Croix-des-Bouquets into sex; he denies the allegations. On 18 Nov 2020 FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him from football for life. On 14 Feb 2023 the Court of Arbitration for Sport annulled the ban; FIFA appealed to the Swiss Federal Tribunal in March 2023 (outcome not checked). Human Rights Watch said witnesses and survivors had faced threats and intimidation. He has not been convicted by any court.

n: New Hampshire Attorney General — Diocese of Manchester (2003)
who: Catholic Diocese of Manchester
cover: The Attorney General cited 'flagrant indifference' to the danger posed by abusive priests and found church officials made false statements while testifying in civil suits; a December 2002 agreement let the diocese avoid criminal indictment after the AG said it had evidence likely to sustain a conviction
d: On 3 March 2003 the New Hampshire Attorney General released a 154-page report, with about 9,000 pages of supporting documents, after a 10-month investigation. It found 50 priests credibly accused of abusing minors over 60 years and cited the diocese's 'flagrant indifference' to the danger to children. Under a December 2002 agreement the diocese avoided criminal indictment, after the Attorney General said it had evidence likely to sustain a conviction against the diocese, and accepted annual monitoring by the Attorney General for at least five years.

n: Pennsylvania grand jury — Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown (2016)
who: Catholic Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown
cover: Two bishops concealed the abuse; the grand jury said the church had such sway over law enforcement that it helped select a police chief
d: A statewide investigating grand jury, in a report released by the Pennsylvania Attorney General on 1 March 2016, found that more than 50 priests and religious leaders abused hundreds of children in the Diocese of Altoona-Johnstown over about 40 years. Two bishops, including Bishop Joseph Adamec, concealed the abuse. The report said the diocese had enough influence over local law enforcement to help choose a police chief.

n: Iowa Attorney General — clergy abuse review (2021)
who: Archdiocese of Dubuque; Dioceses of Des Moines, Davenport and Sioux City; other faith leaders
cover: Survivors told the Attorney General their allegations had been ignored or covered up by the church
d: Iowa Attorney General Tom Miller's office released its review on 23 June 2021 after an inquiry begun in late 2018. It examined 50 complaints, 45 involving the Catholic Church, with records involving 70 priests and alleged abuse from the 1930s to 1997. It described a painful history of abuse and extensive cover-ups in Iowa's Catholic dioceses but found the four dioceses had made reforms in good faith over the past two decades. None of the complaints against Catholic clergy could be prosecuted because of the statute of limitations.

n: New York Attorney General — Diocese of Brooklyn agreement (2024)
who: Catholic Diocese of Brooklyn
cover: The diocese did not consistently follow its own procedures, sometimes did not disclose credible allegations and did not adequately monitor accused clergy; a priest who admitted abusing minors was defrocked in 2007 on condition of confidentiality and this was kept secret until 2017; another priest was moved between parishes after complaints
d: On 16 April 2024 the New York Attorney General announced an agreement after finding that the Diocese of Brooklyn had not consistently followed its own procedures for abuse complaints, applied inconsistent standards of proof and did not adequately monitor credibly accused clergy. In one case a priest who admitted repeatedly abusing minors was removed from duties without parishioners being told, and his 2007 defrocking was kept confidential until 2017; in another a priest was transferred between parishes after earlier concerns and went largely unmonitored despite a 2006 complaint. The diocese accepted new procedures, referral of all complaints to law enforcement and an independent secular monitor for at least three years.

n: Massachusetts Attorney General — Worcester, Fall River and Springfield dioceses (2026)
place: Boston, Massachusetts (Attorney General); dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield
who: Catholic Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield
d: On 30 September 2026 Massachusetts Attorney General Andrea Campbell released a report finding that more than 270 Catholic clergy abused nearly 1,000 children in the Dioceses of Worcester, Fall River and Springfield, with abuse dating back to the 1950s. She called it the first full public accounting of the abuse, misconduct and institutional failures in those dioceses. The report recommended proper investigation of allegations and transparent, accurate records, and Campbell called on Worcester, the only one of the three without a public list of credibly accused priests, to publish one.

n: Daniels review of USA Gymnastics (2017)
who: USA Gymnastics
cover: Reporting rules were so unclear and poorly enforced that the reviewer described the result as 'inadvertent suppression'
d: Former federal prosecutor Deborah Daniels, commissioned by USA Gymnastics in late 2016 after lawsuits over abuse by coaches and team doctor Larry Nassar, released her review on 27 June 2017. She found reporting protocols unclear and poorly enforced, a culture that put performance ahead of protection, and an opaque process for investigating claims. She made 70 recommendations, which the board adopted unanimously.

n: Justice Department finds sexual abuse in five Texas juvenile facilities (2024)
place: Gainesville State School and four other TJJD facilities, Texas
who: Texas Juvenile Justice Department (TJJD)
cover: The US Attorney said Texas state agencies and the Texas Rangers had substantiated sexual abuse allegations at these facilities as early as the 2000s and that the problem persisted
d: On 1 August 2024 the US Justice Department announced findings that the Texas Juvenile Justice Department fails to protect children from sexual abuse by staff and other children at all five of its secure facilities (Evins, Gainesville, Giddings, McLennan County and Ron Jackson), in violation of the Constitution. It also found excessive force, prolonged isolation and inadequate mental-health care. The department noted that state investigations had substantiated sexual abuse at these facilities since the early 2000s.

n: Nova Scotia — Kaufman review of the response to institutional abuse (2002)
who: Nova Scotia provincial youth institutions and the province's compensation programme
d: Retired judge Fred Kaufman, asked by Nova Scotia's government in November 1999 to review its response, delivered 'Searching for Justice: An Independent Review of Nova Scotia's Response to Reports of Institutional Abuse' to Justice Minister Michael Baker on 31 January 2002. The province's compensation programme for people abused in provincial youth institutions, expected to draw about 300 claims, had received 1,264 by the time it closed in 2000 and paid about $39 million in compensation and counselling. Kaufman stated that sexual and physical abuse did occur, but found the programme 'seriously flawed', found significant evidence of false and exaggerated claims, and found that employees were branded as abusers without recourse. He made 105 recommendations.

n: Senate 'Lost Innocents' — child migrants abused in Australian institutions (2001)
place: Bindoon, Western Australia (Christian Brothers' Boys Town)
who: Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia (Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf, Tardun) and other receiving institutions for British and Maltese child migrants
d: The Senate Community Affairs References Committee tabled 'Lost Innocents: Righting the Record — Report on child migration' in August 2001. Of 207 former child migrants who made submissions, 38 described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described 'systemic criminal sexual assault' and predatory behaviour by a large number of Christian Brothers over a long period.

n: Western Australia — St Andrew's Hostel Katanning special inquiry (Blaxell, 2012)
who: St Andrew's Hostel, Katanning (state country high school hostel); warden Dennis McKenna
cover: Most officials who received allegations took no action; the inquiry made adverse findings against a police officer and a local councillor
d: Former judge Peter Blaxell was appointed special inquirer on 22 November 2011 to examine how government agencies and officials responded to allegations of sexual abuse at St Andrew's Hostel, a state-run hostel for rural high-school students. Its warden from 1976 to 1990, Dennis McKenna, was convicted in 1991 of 19 offences against five boys and pleaded guilty in 2011 to 10 more, a total of 29 offences against 11 boys aged 14 to 16. The report, 'How the system and society failed our children', found that most officials took no action on allegations and made adverse findings against one police officer and one local councillor.

n: Spain — Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo audit for the Episcopal Conference (2023)
who: Spanish Episcopal Conference; Catholic clergy, religious and lay church staff
d: The Spanish Episcopal Conference hired the law firm Cremades & Calvo-Sotelo in February 2022 to audit sexual abuse in the Church. The church announced its findings on 21 December 2023: at least 2,056 minor victims and 1,383 complaints, without saying how many clergy were accused. The figure is far below the estimate of more than 200,000 victims since 1940 published in October 2023 by an independent commission appointed by parliament, and the bishops said it was 'obvious that the number is higher'.

n: France — Senate mission on sexual offences against minors by people working with children (2019)
who: Catholic Church in France, sports federations, schools, holiday camps, centres for disabled children
d: A French Senate joint information mission chaired by Catherine Deroche, with Marie Mercier and Michelle Meunier as rapporteurs, presented its conclusions on 29 May 2019 after hearing more than 60 people. Meunier described a 'systemic problem' in the Catholic Church, which the report put down to the sacred status of priests, the lack of checks on power, fear of scandal and a strong culture of secrecy; it flagged centres for disabled minors and sports federations as high-risk. It made 38 recommendations, including checking the sex-offender register (FIJAISV) before every hire to work with minors. A request by Socialist senators for a full commission of inquiry into the Church was refused by the law committee.

n: Germany — Independent Commission case study on child sexual abuse in the GDR (2019)
who: GDR children's homes and Jugendwerkhöfe (youth work homes); families
d: The federal Independent Commission for the Investigation of Child Sexual Abuse presented a case study on the GDR on 6 March 2019, based on the recollections of about 100 men and women abused as children. Girls were more often abused in their own families and boys more often in homes such as the Jugendwerkhöfe (youth work homes). Cases were also documented in which children were organised and sold for sexual services. The study, which is not representative, found that child sexual abuse remained taboo in the GDR considerably longer than in West Germany.

n: Germany — Ettal Benedictine abbey boarding school, IPP study (2013)
who: Benedictine Abbey of Ettal and its boarding school
d: After abuse at the Ettal abbey school became public in 2010, the abbey commissioned the Munich Institute for Practice Research and Project Consulting (IPP; Heiner Keupp, Florian Straus). Its roughly 160-page study, presented on 7 March 2013 and based on 41 interviews with former pupils, relatives and priests and on abbey records, found physical, psychological and sexualised violence over at least three decades, mostly from the 1960s to the 1980s. Keupp described a 'culture of enabling' and said there was no strategic plan or 'System Ettal'.

n: Germany — Diocese of Münster, University of Münster study (2022)
who: Catholic Diocese of Münster
cover: The study found a 'massive leadership failure' under the bishops from 1947 to 2008; most accused priests were transferred rather than restricted.
d: Historians at the University of Münster, including Thomas Großbölting, published a study of the diocese on 13 June 2022 after about two and a half years of research. It found at least 610 minors abused by 196 clerics between 1945 and 2020, about 4% of the diocese's priests in that period, and estimated the real number of victims at 8 to 10 times higher. Bishops and diocesan leaders were often fully informed, covered up cases or intervened only superficially, and usually transferred accused priests.

n: Germany — Diocese of Essen, IPP study (2023)
who: Catholic Diocese of Essen
cover: Accused priests were often moved to other posts, sometimes in other dioceses; parishes were not informed, and until 2010 the diocese made no effort to support victims.
d: The Munich IPP institute, with the Berlin institute Dissens, published its study of the diocese's 65 years on 14 February 2023. It found 226 people who reported abuse and 190 accused clergy in the records, with most offences in the 1950s to 1970s. Accused priests were often reassigned, sometimes to other dioceses, without parishes being told, and until 2010 the diocese did nothing to support victims. Bishop Franz-Josef Overbeck acknowledged the failures; about 1.9 million euros had been paid to victims.

n: Austria — Kremsmünster Abbey school abuse, diocesan commission and IPP study
who: Benedictine Abbey of Kremsmünster and its Stiftsgymnasium
d: Abuse at the boarding school of the Benedictine abbey of Kremsmünster in Upper Austria became public in 2010. In July 2013 an Austrian court sentenced a former priest who had been the boarding-school director to 12 years in prison for abusing 24 boys in the 1970s, 1980s and 1990s. A study by the Munich Institute for Practice Research (IPP), commissioned by the abbey and published in March 2015, drew on interviews covering 1945 to 2000 and identified 350 cases of sexual, physical or psychological violence and 24 accused people.

n: Diocese of Passau — University of Passau study (2025)
who: Catholic Diocese of Passau — priests, deacons and religious brothers
cover: Bishops and vicars general often put protecting the institution and the priesthood above victims; judges, prosecutors, medical experts and school and youth authorities are named as bystanders.
d: A University of Passau team led by historian Marc von Knorring, commissioned by the diocese's independent review commission, published its study online on 8 December 2025 covering 1945 to 2022. It found at least 672 minors, mostly boys, who were sexually abused or physically mistreated (or both) by 154 clergy, about 6.4% of some 2,400 priests, deacons and religious clergy in the period; 128 of them sexually abused minors, and about 86% were likely repeat offenders. Abuse took place in boarding schools and homes, religious lessons and altar-server duties. The study found bishops and vicars general often protected the institution and the priesthood rather than victims.

n: Diocese of Fulda — independent review commission final report (2025)
who: Catholic Diocese of Fulda; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp (personnel chief 1977–2003)
cover: Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently to protect the church's reputation and transferred without stated reasons; victims were ignored until 2010.
d: The independent commission for the Diocese of Fulda, chaired by former Fulda mayor Gerhard Möller, presented its final report on 17 June 2025 after reviewing 2,124 files covering about 80 years. It identified 120 victims and 37 accused priests and chaplains, with 239 provable sexual offences, and said the true number is several times higher. Until about 2000 accused clergy were treated leniently and moved without explanation, and victims were ignored until 2010; auxiliary bishop Johannes Kapp, in charge of personnel from 1977 to 2003, was named as mainly responsible. Bishop Michael Gerber said the diocese had incurred guilt and church structures had failed.

n: Salesians of Don Bosco, German Province — working group report (2011)
who: Salesians of Don Bosco, German Province — homes and schools
d: A working group with internal and external members set up by the German Province of the Salesians of Don Bosco reported on 23 February 2011. It had received 120 complaints concerning Salesian facilities from 1950 into the 1980s, about half about sexual abuse and half about physical violence, against members of the order and employees. About two-thirds of the cases had been clarified, and cases were referred to prosecutors.

n: German Franciscan Province — IPP study (2026)
who: German Franciscan Province (OFM) — educational institutions incl. Vossenack school and boarding school
d: The Munich IPP institute, led by Peter Caspari, presented its study for the German Franciscan Province on 25 February 2026, covering the period since 1945. It identified more than 100 victims, mostly minors aged 10 to 15 when the abuse began and about three-quarters male, and 98 suspected perpetrators; most abuse took place in educational institutions. The provincial minister acknowledged structural problems and the order's guilt. A survivor from the Vossenack school accused the leadership of years of cover-up.

n: Korntal Brüdergemeinde children's homes — final report (2018)
who: Evangelische Brüdergemeinde Korntal — three children's homes in Korntal and Wilhelmsdorf
d: Retired judge Brigitte Baums-Stammberger and educational scientist Benno Hafeneger presented their 400-page report 'Uns wurde die Würde genommen' in Stuttgart on 7 June 2018, after 115 interviews with former residents. Of the 105 accounts used, 56 reported sexualised violence and 93 physical violence in three homes of the Protestant Brüdergemeinde in Korntal and Wilhelmsdorf from 1949 to the 1980s. A caretaker forced at least 30 children into sexual acts; a stable worker, a baker and a children's doctor were also named as serious offenders. The Brüdergemeinde apologised and paid recognition payments, usually 5,000 euros.

n: Saarland University Hospital (UKS) — independent review commission (2023)
who: Universitätsklinikum des Saarlandes, Homburg — an assistant physician (died 2016) and hospital leadership
cover: The hospital and prosecutors decided not to inform potentially affected families; relatives and the public learned of the suspicions only in 2019.
d: An independent commission chaired by former BKA president Jörg Ziercke presented its final report on 24 May 2023 on suspected abuse at Saarland University Hospital. An assistant physician carried out medically unnecessary intimate examinations of children between 2010 and 2014; the hospital reported him at the end of 2014 and dismissed him, and the investigation ended when he died in 2016. The commission confirmed 52 of more than 80 suspected cases and found a lack of consistent leadership; the decision by the hospital and prosecutors not to inform families until 2019 was the main cause of lost trust. It recommended compensation of 5,000 to 50,000 euros per case.

n: Vienna — historians' commission (2012) and Weisser Ring support programme for victims of city youth welfare (2010–2019)
who: City of Vienna youth welfare — municipal, church and private children's homes and foster care, incl. the Kinderübernahmestelle (KÜST)
d: A historians' commission led by Reinhard Sieder reported in May 2012 on Vienna's municipal, church and private children's homes after 1945, through which roughly 100,000 children passed; it described sadistic sexual abuse by some staff alongside widespread violence. The City of Vienna commissioned the victim-support organisation Weisser Ring in 2010 to handle claims of people harmed in Vienna youth welfare institutions between 1945 and 1999. Its final report (2019) records 3,139 reports and financial aid to 2,384 people, with 42.13 million euros paid directly to victims. The separate Wilhelminenberg commission is already on the map.

n: Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI) — national safeguarding reports (2022–2025)
who: Conferenza Episcopale Italiana — diocesan listening centres and the national child-protection service
cover: Critics, including Rete l'Abuso, said the reports cover only recent diocesan-desk data and omit court and Vatican cases; the first report mentions no reports to civil authorities.
d: The Italian Bishops' Conference published its first national report in November 2022, prepared with experts of the Università Cattolica: 80 diocesan listening centres had received 86 contacts in 2020–2021 concerning 89 people, against 68 alleged abusers, 44% of them clerics. CEI also said dioceses had sent 613 files on clerics to the Vatican's doctrine office since 2000. Its third survey, presented in May 2025, counted 115 alleged victims (64 boys, 51 girls) and 67 alleged perpetrators, 44 of them clergy, in 2023–2024. Critics said the reports are too narrow and Italy has no independent national inquiry.

n: Mallorca — Consell de Mallorca commission on sexual exploitation of children in IMAS care (2021)
who: Institut Mallorquí d'Afers Socials (IMAS), the island's child-protection agency
d: A commission of the Consell de Mallorca, chaired by vice-president Jaume Tortella, reported on 23 April 2021 on the sexual exploitation of minors in the care of the island's child-protection agency IMAS; about 16 cases were known in January 2020, 13 of them from 2017 to early 2019. With the PP and Vox refusing to take part, it found no political, technical or criminal responsibility and no network linking the cases, matching the prosecutors' investigation. Reporting had changed in February 2020 so that suspicions go to the national police, and five cases not previously reported were sent to prosecutors. In late 2020 two men were convicted of corrupting girls in care, and in April 2022 a European Parliament Petitions Committee delegation visited Palma to examine the cases.

n: Malta — Church Response Team figures on clergy abuse 1991–2010
who: Catholic Church in Malta — Response Team set up by the Maltese bishops (chair Judge Victor Caruana Colombo)
d: In April 2010 the Maltese Curia said the Church's Response Team, set up by the bishops in 1991 and chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 remained open, four priests were found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. The convictions over St Joseph Home are already on the map.

n: Australian Defence Force — HMAS Leeuwin, Balcombe and ADF Cadets (Royal Commission Case Study 40)
who: Royal Australian Navy (HMAS Leeuwin), Army Apprentice School Balcombe, Australian Air Force Cadets
cover: Senior staff at HMAS Leeuwin knew of the abuse and tolerated it; in 2000 a 15-year-old Air Force cadet faced disciplinary proceedings and discharge after an adult instructor's inappropriate relationship with her, which the commission said should never have happened.
d: The Royal Commission's Case Study 40 report (23 August 2017) found that physical and sexual abuse of child recruits was widespread at the navy base HMAS Leeuwin from the 1960s to 1972, that senior staff knew and tolerated it, and that the navy failed in its duty of care. At the Army Apprentice School, Balcombe, in the 1970s and 1980s an unofficial rank hierarchy let senior apprentices sexually and physically abuse junior ones. In the Air Force Cadets, policies from at least 2000 gave the age of consent as 14, which the commission said increased the risk of abuse. In June 2014 the Defence Abuse Response Taskforce had reported allegations from more than 200 junior recruits aged 15 to 17 at HMAS Leeuwin.

n: Australia — 'The Forgotten Children': national inquiry into children in immigration detention
place: Sydney (seat of the Australian Human Rights Commission)
who: Australian Government immigration detention (onshore centres and Nauru regional processing centre)
d: The Australian Human Rights Commission's national inquiry, 'The Forgotten Children', was tabled in Federal Parliament on 11 February 2015. It reported 33 incidents of reported sexual assault in immigration detention between January 2013 and March 2014, 'the vast majority involving children'. A separate government-commissioned review by Philip Moss (March 2015) on the Nauru centre was aware of three rape allegations, one involving a minor, and confirmed that a guard demanded to see a female detainee naked in exchange for extra shower time with her young child.

n: Tasmania — Ombudsman's review of claims of abuse in state care, 'Listen to the Children' (2004)
who: Tasmanian state care: state, church and charitable homes (including Ashley, Rochebank, Clarendon, Kennerley, Glenara and Mt St Canice) and foster care
d: After a former state ward spoke publicly in July 2003 about abuse in state care, the Tasmanian Ombudsman reviewed claims from adults who had been abused as children in state care, publishing 'Listen to the Children' in November 2004 and a Phase 2 final report in June 2006. The review covered state, church and charitable homes and foster care, where sexual abuse from the 1950s to the 1970s had been described. It led to the state's Abuse in State Care program (2003–2013), which accepted 1,848 claimants and paid between $35,000 and $60,000 each. Claimants who accepted a payment had to waive future legal action against the government. Tasmania's 2023 Commission of Inquiry later found that allegations against staff and carers revealed through the program had not been acted on.

n: Rotherham — IOPC Operation Linden report on South Yorkshire Police (2022)
who: South Yorkshire Police
cover: IOPC found significant failures by South Yorkshire Police to protect children from organised grooming; 8 officers had a case to answer for misconduct and 6 for gross misconduct; 43 of 164 complaint allegations were upheld
d: The Independent Office for Police Conduct published its Operation Linden report on 22 June 2022, after 91 investigations (begun 2014–2018) into South Yorkshire Police's response to child sexual exploitation in Rotherham from 1997 to 2013. The investigations covered 265 allegations from 51 complainants, 44 of them survivors, and the conduct of 47 officers. Eight officers had a case to answer for misconduct and six for gross misconduct; many had retired, five officers received sanctions from management action to a final written warning, and a sixth officer's misconduct case was found not proven at a 2022 hearing. The IOPC found the force was not equipped to deal with organised grooming at the scale it met in Rotherham and failed to protect vulnerable children.

n: IICSA — sexual abuse in residential, boarding, music and special schools (2022)
who: Boarding schools, residential special schools and specialist music schools in England and Wales; school inspectorates and the Teaching Regulation Agency
d: IICSA's residential schools report (March 2022, over 220 pages) covered music and residential special schools in phase 1 and day and boarding schools in phase 2. It found that boarding pupils, children with special needs and pupils in one-to-one music teaching were especially exposed to abuse by adults and peers, and that school reputations were sometimes put before victims. It found weaknesses in inspection, teacher regulation and DBS checks and made recommendations in seven areas.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Morrison's Academy, Crieff
who: Morrison's Academy boarding houses
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry's eleventh set of findings, published on 5 March 2024, covered boarding at Morrison's Academy from 1945 to 2007, when it stopped taking boarders. Lady Smith found children were abused, mainly physically and emotionally, with some sexual abuse, including by a few older pupils. Boarding houses could operate as separate 'fiefdoms' without adequate oversight by school management until the 1990s, and a strong culture of not reporting discouraged children from speaking up.

n: Kerelaw residential school and secure unit, Stevenston — Frizzell inquiry
who: Kerelaw residential school and secure unit, run by Glasgow City Council from 1996
d: The Scottish Government commissioned Eddie Frizzell to inquire into Kerelaw in November 2007; his report was published in May 2009. It found abuse did take place, physical abuse was prevalent, complaints were not consistently followed up, and there were significant failures of management and leadership linked to Glasgow City Council's neglect of the school. Two staff were convicted in 2006, one receiving 10 years for 18 offences, and 14 staff were dismissed. The council had reported 350–400 allegations from 159 people.

n: Clwyd children's homes — Jillings report (1996, published 2013)
who: Clwyd County Council children's homes; North Wales Police
cover: Compiled in 1996 but withheld for 17 years; the panel said agencies gave limited information and sometimes refused to meet it; North Wales Police investigated allegations against its own officers.
d: John Jillings led an investigation into abuse in Clwyd County Council's children's homes; the report was finished in 1996, withheld because the council's insurers feared compensation claims, and published in redacted form in July 2013. It found abuse in Clwyd homes was 'extensive and has taken place over a substantial number of years' and that responses were 'too little and too late'. It criticised North Wales Police for investigating allegations against its own officers and said the council and other agencies gave limited information, some refusing to meet the panel. It called for a judicial inquiry; the Waterhouse tribunal later examined the wider abuse.

n: Utting review 'People Like Us' — safeguards for children living away from home (1997)
place: England and Wales (Department of Health, London)
who: Children's homes, foster care, boarding and special schools, penal institutions in England and Wales
d: After allegations of widespread ill-treatment in children's homes dating back to the 1970s, the government asked Sir William Utting, former chief inspector of social services, to review safeguards for all children living away from home. His 1997 report found safeguards stronger than a decade earlier but said children in prison and in private foster care were not properly protected and that abuse of disabled children was overlooked; it called persistent sexual abusers 'a scourge of childhood'. It made 159 recommendations, leading to the Quality Protects programme.

n: Children's Commissioner for England — inquiry into sexual exploitation in gangs and groups (2012–13)
place: England (Office of the Children's Commissioner, London)
who: Gangs and groups sexually exploiting children across England
d: The Office of the Children's Commissioner's inquiry, supported by the University of Bedfordshire, published interim findings on 21 November 2012. It identified 2,409 children confirmed as victims of sexual exploitation by gangs and groups in the 14 months from August 2010 to October 2011, and a further 16,500 at risk. It recorded 1,514 perpetrators of varied ethnicity (545 white, 415 Asian, 244 black, the rest not recorded) and listed warning signs professionals should act on, such as running away, self-harm and repeated sexually transmitted infections. The final report followed in 2013.

n: Manchester — Operation Augusta assurance review (2020)
