who: Greater Manchester Police; Manchester City Council children's homes; groups of men exploiting girls in care
cover: Senior officers closed the investigation in July 2005; minutes of the meetings on its closure disappeared and several officials declined to cooperate with the review.
d: An assurance review commissioned by Greater Manchester Mayor Andy Burnham, published 14 January 2020, found that Operation Augusta, set up in 2004 after the death of a 15-year-old girl in council care, had identified at least 57 victims and 97 potential suspects before senior officers closed it in July 2005. Allegations of rape and abuse were not followed up and very few perpetrators were brought to justice; some suspects visited council children's homes apparently with staff knowledge. Minutes of the closure meetings were missing.

n: Ireland — National Board's safeguarding reviews of every Catholic diocese and order (2011–2017), incl. Raphoe
place: All dioceses on the island of Ireland (National Board, Maynooth); Raphoe review covers Co. Donegal
who: Catholic dioceses and religious congregations in Ireland and Northern Ireland; National Board for Safeguarding Children in the Catholic Church
cover: Raphoe: the review found 'significant' errors by bishops, with frequent delays in reporting allegations or none at all, and victims' needs ignored to protect the Church's reputation (Bishop Boyce's statement).
d: The Catholic Church's National Board for Safeguarding Children reviewed every diocese on the island of Ireland and the religious orders that ran schools and institutions, publishing in tranches from 30 November 2011 to 2017. The first tranche included Raphoe, where 52 allegations had been made against 14 priests since 1975 and four had been convicted; Bishop Philip Boyce accepted 'very poor judgements and mistakes'. A December 2013 tranche reported, for example, 67 allegations against 21 priests in Kerry and 59 against 42 in Down and Connor.

n: Denmark — Appeals Board finds 'systematic illegal behaviour' in Korean adoptions 1970–1989
who: Danish adoption agencies DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp (and Terre des Hommes); South Korean agencies
cover: Two Danish agencies knew that children's information was being changed.
d: A report released in January 2024 by Denmark's Appeals Board (Ankestyrelsen), which supervises intercountry adoption, examined adoptions from South Korea between 1970 and 1989, when 7,220 children were adopted to Denmark. It found 'systematic illegal behaviour' on the Korean side: weak regulation let organisations alter adoptees' identities and backgrounds in official documents, and large sums of money passed between organisations in the two countries. It found that DanAdopt and AC Børnehjælp knew about the changing of children's information. Adoptee groups said it did not examine the Danish state's role.

n: Finland — Conservative Laestadian movement (SRK) admits 70–100 child abuse cases mishandled
who: Central Committee of Conservative Laestadian Congregations (SRK), Finland's largest revivalist movement within the Lutheran church
cover: SRK admitted officials 'mishandled' cases, did not use expert help and did not communicate, which could look like downplaying or covering up.
d: In April 2011 the SRK, which has about 35,000 members, announced that an internal report had found 70 to 100 cases of child sexual abuse within the movement since the 1980s. Most involved abuse within member families rather than by church officials, but the SRK admitted its officials had mishandled the cases and lacked the knowledge to respond. A study by Johanna Hurtig (University of Tampere) on abuse in the movement was published the same year.

n: Yemen — UN Group of Eminent Experts: rape of boys and girls by armed forces; sexual violence against recruited girls
place: Aden (Security Belt Forces facilities); also Ta'izz, Sana'a, Ibb
who: Security Belt Forces; Yemeni 35th Armoured Brigade; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa; Houthi de facto authorities
d: The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 (A/HRC/42/17) that Security Belt Forces raped 18 women, four boys and a girl in 2016–2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden; members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy; and Houthi detention sites saw sexual violence against a 17-year-old boy. Its September 2020 report found credible accounts that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13–17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.

n: Zimbabwe — Gender Commission inquiry into sexual exploitation of girls and child marriage in apostolic sects (2021–2023)
place: Harare (Zimbabwe Gender Commission); sect sites in Marange and Marondera
who: Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect and other apostolic church branches
d: After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect shrine in August 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened a public investigation on 24 September 2021 into sexual exploitation and abuse of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects. It identified compulsory virginity testing, wife pledging, betrothal and forced marriage in the Marange sect, and an earlier 2020 probe of branches around Marondera found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as 'wives-in-waiting' and married at puberty. Its report for 2022 said it had received and investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation and called for legislation regulating faith-based organisations.

n: Argentina — CONADEP 'Nunca Más': children of the disappeared taken and given to military families (1984)
who: Argentine armed and security forces (1976–83)
cover: Identities of children changed; records of births in detention not kept
d: The National Commission on the Disappearance of Persons, created by President Raúl Alfonsín on 15 December 1983 and chaired by Ernesto Sábato, delivered its report Nunca Más on 20 September 1984. It recorded 8,960 forced disappearances between 1976 and 1983 and stated that no fewer than 200 children under 15 had been kidnapped; babies were taken with their parents or born to pregnant prisoners in detention camps and given to military families. The report was key evidence in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas.

n: Jamaica — Keating Report on children in state care finds sexual abuse by caregivers (2003)
who: Jamaican children's homes and places of safety; Child Services Division
cover: Nine of 15 homes visited could not recall an official inspection in the previous three years
d: The Government of Jamaica appointed a four-member review panel chaired by Sadie Keating in December 2002, after a public campaign about abuse in children's homes. Its report, reported by the Jamaica Observer on 15 July 2003, found that children in homes and places of safety had been sexually abused, including by care-giving staff, and that nine of the 15 homes visited could not recall a Child Services Division inspection in the past three years.

n: Special Court for Sierra Leone — RUF leaders convicted of sexual slavery, forced marriage and use of child soldiers (2009)
who: Revolutionary United Front (RUF): Issa Sesay, Morris Kallon, Augustine Gbao
d: On 25 February 2009 the Special Court for Sierra Leone convicted RUF leaders Issa Sesay and Morris Kallon on 16 of 18 counts and Augustine Gbao on 14. All three were convicted of sexual slavery and of forced marriage as a crime against humanity, the first forced-marriage convictions by an international criminal tribunal; Sesay and Kallon were also convicted of using child soldiers, while Gbao was acquitted of that charge. They were sentenced to 52, 40 and 25 years, and on 26 October 2009 the Appeals Chamber upheld the convictions and sentences, overturning only Gbao's conviction for collective punishments.

n: Central African Republic — Deschamps panel finds 'gross institutional failure' by the UN over child abuse by foreign troops (2015)
who: French Sangaris forces; Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA soldiers; UN officials who handled the allegations
cover: Report passed 'from inbox to inbox'; panel found abuse of authority by the head of MINUSCA's Human Rights and Justice Section, the SRSG for MINUSCA and the head of OIOS, and that staff became more concerned with whether the allegations had been improperly leaked to French authorities than with acting on them
d: The External Independent Review Panel appointed by the Secretary-General and chaired by Marie Deschamps reported on 17 December 2015. It examined accounts by boys aged about 8 to 13 sheltering at the M'Poko camp in Bangui that soldiers, largely from the French Sangaris force, and also Chadian and Equatorial Guinean MISCA troops, had sexually abused them between December 2013 and June 2014, often in exchange for food or money. It called the UN's handling a 'gross institutional failure' and found that three senior UN officials had abused their authority.

n: Malaysia — government task force confirms rape of Penan schoolgirls by timber workers in Sarawak (2009)
who: Workers of Malaysian logging companies in Sarawak (no company named)
cover: Sarawak police said three complaints the year before had been probed and none taken to court
d: A team from Malaysia's Ministry of Women, Family and Community Development investigated in Sarawak in November 2008, and its report, made public in September 2009 after the Associated Press obtained it, found that timber workers had raped or tried to sexually abuse Penan schoolgirls, some as young as 10, including girls given lifts to school in logging trucks. The team interviewed four women with direct experience and many others who said abuse was common; it named no company. Sarawak police said three complaints had been investigated the previous year without enough evidence to prosecute.

n: Welcome to Video — darknet CSAM site run from South Korea
who: Welcome to Video (operator Son Jong-woo / Son Jung-woo)
cover: South Korean courts gave the operator 18 months on appeal (May 2019); Seoul High Court refused US extradition on 6 July 2020.
d: A Korean-run darknet site that sold access to child sexual abuse videos for Bitcoin; it held over 250,000 unique videos and its server had more than one million Bitcoin addresses, one per account. IRS-CI tracing of Bitcoin transactions located the server in South Korea, and the operator, Son Jong-woo, was arrested on 5 March 2018. On 16 October 2019 the US DOJ announced 337 users arrested and charged, with leads sent to 38 countries (Korean police counted 310 arrests in 32 countries, 223 of them Koreans). He served 18 months in South Korea; on 6 July 2020 the Seoul High Court refused US extradition, and in July 2022 he received a further 24 months for concealing proceeds. DOJ said 45% of the videos analysed had not been known before.

n: Operation Rescue — Boylover forum network
who: Boylover forum (Netherlands-hosted)
d: A forum presenting itself as 'discussion-only' where members made contact before moving to private channels to share abuse images. UK CEOP traced the owner and the server to the Netherlands in 2009; Europol rebuilt the forum offline and sent 4,202 intelligence reports to 25 EU states and 8 other countries. By March 2011, 670 suspects had been identified, 184 arrested and 230 children safeguarded, which Europol called the highest number for such an investigation.

n: Elysium darknet platform
place: Bad Camberg, Hesse (servers); trial at Limburg
who: Elysium (darknet forum and chats, over 87,000 members)
d: Elysium existed from late 2016 and was used to exchange abuse material and to arrange the sexual abuse of children; it had German, French, Spanish and Italian chat groups. German prosecutors (ZIT Frankfurt) and the BKA shut it down in June 2017 after Australian police passed on a lead; 14 suspects were arrested, 12 suspected of abusing children themselves. On 7 March 2019 the Limburg court sentenced four men to between 3 years 10 months and 9 years 9 months, with preventive detention for the main administrator.

n: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
d: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.

n: Europol sprint on buyers of live-distant abuse in the Philippines (2024)
place: The Hague (sprint); victims in the Philippines
who: Buyers worldwide directing livestreamed abuse by traffickers in the Philippines
d: From 24 to 28 June 2024, 32 investigators at Europol processed leads from US HSI investigations into networks exploiting children in the Philippines: over 10 million lines of chat between about 12,000 customer accounts and 100 seller accounts, built up over 12 years. The sprint produced information packages that may lead authorities in 24 countries to 197 buyers. Europol notes buyers direct traffickers to abuse children in real time on webcam and some travel to the Philippines to abuse children in person.

n: Ogoshi brothers — Nigeria-based sextortion of a Michigan teenager
who: Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, Lagos (convicted); Ezekiel Ejehem Robert (charged)
d: Men in Lagos used hacked Instagram accounts, posing as a girl, to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan and demanded $1,000; he died by suicide in March 2022. A federal grand jury indicted the brothers in November 2022; they were extradited from Nigeria in August 2023. The indictment said they tried to extort more than 100 people. They pleaded guilty to conspiracy to sexually exploit teenage boys (announced 10 April 2024) and were each sentenced to 17.5 years in September 2024. A third defendant, Ezekiel Robert, appealed a Nigerian extradition order; charges against him remain pending.

n: A.M. v. Omegle — site shut after child exploitation lawsuit
who: Omegle (random video chat)
d: A plaintiff known in court documents as A.M., paired at age 11 on Omegle with an adult man who then sexually exploited her for three years (he was jailed for eight years in Canada), filed a lawsuit in November 2021 alleging the site paired minors with predators; she had sought $22 million at a jury trial. BBC reported Omegle had been mentioned in more than 50 cases against paedophiles in the previous couple of years. On 8 November 2023 founder Leif K-Brooks announced the site's closure; under an out-of-court settlement for an undisclosed sum, which A.M. said included closure, he added the line 'I thank A.M. for opening my eyes to the human cost of Omegle' with a link to the lawsuit.

n: Apple cancels iCloud Photos CSAM scanning plan
who: Apple Inc.
d: In August 2021 Apple announced a plan to scan photos stored in iCloud for known child sexual abuse material on users' devices. After criticism from privacy and security researchers it paused the plan, and on 7 December 2022 told Wired it had decided not to move forward with the CSAM detection tool for iCloud Photos, focusing instead on its opt-in 'Communication Safety' features for children's accounts. Wikipedia reports that Apple had scanned iCloud Mail attachments for abuse imagery since 2019.

n: Australia: eSafety Commissioner, Online Safety Act 2021 and under-16 social media ban
who: Office of the eSafety Commissioner
d: Australia's Online Safety Act 2021 (Act No. 76 of 2021) gives the eSafety Commissioner removal and transparency powers over online services. On 28 November 2024 parliament approved a ban on children under 16 using social media, to be enforced by the eSafety regulator with fines of up to A$50 million for non-compliant companies, taking effect at least 12 months later. Wikipedia reports that Roblox, initially excluded, was to be covered by protocols from March 2026, and that in June 2020 Australia passed the Crimes Legislation Amendment (Sexual Crimes Against Children and Community Protection Measures) Act, which IJM said recognised Australians' role in demand for livestreamed abuse.

n: Landslide Productions / Operations Avalanche and Ore
who: Landslide Productions (payment portal, Thomas and Janice Reedy)
cover: Later reconstruction of the Landslide data found many listed names were victims of credit-card fraud, and the validity of UK Operation Ore procedures was questioned; an estimated 33 suicides followed in the UK.
d: Landslide, a Fort Worth, Texas portal run by Thomas and Janice Reedy, processed credit-card sign-ups for third-party sites, some offering child abuse images. US agents raided it in August 1999; a jury convicted Thomas Reedy, who was sentenced to 1,335 years (reduced to 180 on appeal), and Janice Reedy got 14 years. US Operation Avalanche examined about 35,000 names on the database, and the FBI passed details of 7,272 British residents to UK police, starting Operation Ore, Britain's biggest computer crime investigation; raids began in May 2002. CEOP said 140 children had been rescued in the UK. Later forensic examination showed large-scale credit card fraud in Landslide's records (54,348 sets of stolen card details), and some people were wrongly accused; a legal challenge in 2009 argued that many convictions for incitement rested on flawed credit-card evidence. Follow-on operations took place in other countries.

n: Austria-led 2007 investigation — 2,360 suspects in 77 countries
who: Online distribution network uncovered by Austrian authorities
cover: The two Irish suspects were not investigated by the Garda until six months after Austria notified them.
d: The investigation began in July 2006 when an employee of a Vienna-based file-hosting service reported suspicious material; within 24 hours investigators recorded more than 8,000 hits from 2,361 IP addresses in 77 countries. On 7 February 2007 Austrian authorities announced more than 2,360 suspects who had paid to view videos of young children being sexually abused; the FBI was investigating about 600, about 130 were Australian, France was looking at about 100 and at least 23 were Austrian. Germany had the largest number of suspects. No suspects were yet in custody at the announcement.

n: Operation Lobos / Baby Heart (Brazil-led)
who: Baby Heart and other Tor boards
d: A year-long global investigation into the Tor child-abuse site 'Babyheart' and its administrator involved the UK NCA and West Midlands Police, Australian Federal Police and Queensland's Task Force Argos, Toronto Police, the Brazilian Federal Police, INTERPOL, Europol and US ICE, with nine countries listed (Australia, Austria, Brazil, Canada, France, Italy, Portugal, the US and the UK). Intelligence narrowed the administrator's location to Portugal, where the Portuguese Judicial Police arrested and charged him in 2017; examination of his devices identified seven victims directly related to him. INTERPOL and Portuguese police presented the case publicly on 23 January 2020. Brazil's Federal Police ran related 'Operação Lobos' phases.

n: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
d: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

n: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
d: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

n: Operación Roblox — extortion network in Panama
who: A man in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera (Panamá Oeste), arrested in 'Operación Roblox'
d: On 23 October 2024 Panama's National Police and Public Ministry carried out 'Operación Roblox' in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera district, arresting a man accused of illicit contact with minors through the Roblox gaming platform and of threatening them to demand child sexual abuse material. The alert came from Spanish police investigating a child sexual abuse material network; phones and laptops were seized and investigations were continuing.

n: Operation Long Arm — 'Bamse' bulletin board (1992)
who: Bamse BBS (Danish bulletin board, ~900 users)
d: US Customs' first major case against internet child abuse material. In late 1992 a US Customs controlled delivery led to a suspect who said he had obtained images from a Europe-based bulletin board; agents found 'Bamse', a Danish bulletin board with child abuse rooms, and two other Danish boards using its images, where users paid a subscription or supplied images of their own. Working with Danish authorities, the operation led to about 35 arrests and convictions in the US. Start year approximate.

n: Spanish town: boys made AI nude images of 20 girls
who: Teenage boys using a 'nudify' website
d: In September 2023, at the start of the school year in Almendralejo (Extremadura), AI-generated nude images of schoolgirls made with an app circulated in at least four of the town's five middle schools; more than 20 girls were affected, including girls aged 12 and 14. Police received at least seven complaints and identified several of the alleged authors, and the case was referred to the Juvenile Prosecutor's Office.

n: Operation Stovewood — NCA Rotherham investigation
who: National Crime Agency investigation into non-recent exploitation in Rotherham
d: The National Crime Agency took over the Rotherham investigation in 2014. Its page reports about 1,150 potential victims identified, more than 220 people arrested or interviewed voluntarily, and 39 people convicted with about 470 years of prison sentences. On 8 August 2025 the NCA agreed to take over an investigation, directed by the Independent Office for Police Conduct, into allegations of child sexual abuse by former South Yorkshire Police officers (allegations; no finding yet).

n: Newcastle — Operation Sanctuary
who: Grooming networks; Northumbria Police
d: Operation Sanctuary began in 2014 and led to 18 people being jailed for sexually abusing girls and young women they had groomed in Newcastle. The Joint Serious Case Review, published 23 February 2018, put the number of victims at about 700 across the Northumbria area, 108 of them in Newcastle. It found no evidence that concerns about political correctness or accusations of racism made police reluctant to investigate, and called for law changes on sexual exploitation.

n: Keighley — 2016 convictions
who: Grooming network
d: In February 2016 twelve men were jailed, with sentences of up to 20 years, for sexually exploiting a vulnerable teenage girl in Keighley. A further six men were jailed in 2022 for the systematic rape of another teenage girl in the town.

n: Independent Inquiry into Grooming Gangs (2025–)
who: National panel overseeing local investigations
d: On 9 December 2025 the Home Secretary named Baroness Anne Longfield, former Children's Commissioner, as chair of a national inquiry with full statutory powers overseeing local investigations into grooming gangs, following Casey's recommendation. It is time-limited to three years with a £65m budget, will hold individuals and institutions to account, and Oldham is the first confirmed local investigation. Final terms of reference were due by March 2026.

n: FBI Operation Cross Country XIII (2023)
who: FBI and partner agencies
d: During a two-week operation in July 2023, announced 1 August 2023, the FBI and partners identified and located 200 sex-trafficking victims, including 59 minor victims of child sex trafficking and sexual exploitation, and located 59 actively missing children. 68 trafficking suspects and 126 suspects of child sexual exploitation and trafficking offences were identified or arrested.

n: Netherlands — National Rapporteur estimate of exploited Dutch girls
who: Domestic pimps and 'loverboy' recruiters
d: A report by National Rapporteur Corinne Dettmeijer, prepared with UNODC and published 18 October 2017, estimated that at least 1,320 underage Dutch girls aged 12 to 17 fall victim to sexual exploitation in the Netherlands each year, using 2012–2016 data. Underage girls made up nearly half of female victims in the Dutch sex industry. In October 2025 the current rapporteur reported reported exploitation cases rising from 868 (2023) to 944 (2024), with more teenage victims.

n: Black Axe in Palermo — 14 convicted (2018), 4 acquitted of mafia association (2019)
who: Black Axe (Nigerian confraternity) cell in Palermo
d: A Palermo police operation on 18 November 2016 arrested 19 alleged members of a Black Axe cell based in the Ballarò district; prosecutors said it ran debt collection, exploitation of prostitution and drug trafficking with mafia-style initiation rites. On 21 May 2018 a Palermo judge (fast-track procedure) convicted 14 Nigerians to a combined 87 years. In November 2019 the Palermo Corte d'Assise, trying five others, did not accept the mafia-association charge: four were acquitted and one was jailed for 11 years for kidnapping and sexual violence.

n: Libya — sex trafficking of sub-Saharan girls in southern brothels; abuse of transiting children (US TIP 2025)
who: Commercial sex rings; armed groups; officials
cover: Observers report systemic official complicity, including Libyan Coast Guard, immigration and security officials; the government has never reported prosecuting or convicting anyone for sex or labour trafficking.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says commercial sex rings subject sub-Saharan women and girls to sex trafficking in brothels, particularly in Ubari, Sabha and Murzuq, and that Nigerian women and girls are at increased risk. It cites an international organization finding that 77 per cent of children and youth transiting Libya experienced indicators of exploitation amounting to trafficking.

n: Lake Volta, Ghana — child trafficking in fishing (IJM prevalence study 2023)
who: Fishing-boat owners and intermediaries on Lake Volta
d: A 2023 International Justice Mission household survey of 1,286 children in three fishing districts around Lake Volta estimated that about 37.7 per cent were likely trafficked and a further 45.1 per cent were in likely exploitative child labour. The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit children as young as four in Lake Volta's fishing industry, controlling them with violence and limited food, and that girls in the fishing sector are vulnerable to sexual exploitation; it notes observers reported forced child labour on the lake has decreased.

n: Kenya — child sex trafficking in Kilifi/Kwale villas; Karamoja girls to Nairobi (US TIP 2025)
who: Family members, taxi drivers, recruiters; foreign and local offenders
cover: The report notes ongoing concerns of official complicity with no reported action against complicit officials.
d: The 2025 US TIP report cites a 2023 NGO study estimating that more than 2,000 children were exploited in child sex trafficking in Kilifi and Kwale counties, increasingly in private villas and vacation homes rather than hotels. It also reports cross-border rings moving women and underage girls from Uganda's Karamoja region to Nairobi, and truck drivers, miners and Lake Victoria fishermen exploiting children.

n: Morocco — foreign offenders in Tangier vacation rentals (US TIP 2025)
who: Foreign nationals, primarily from Europe and the Middle East
d: The 2025 US TIP report says some foreign nationals, primarily from Europe and the Middle East, sexually exploit children in major Moroccan cities, and NGOs report tourists exploit children in Tangier in vacation rentals owned and managed by European nationals. It also reports alleged exploitation of children after the September 2023 Al Haouz earthquake. Courts convicted 60 traffickers in 2024.

n: Mozambique — girls exploited along the Maputo–South Africa highway and at mines (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers at rest stops, bars, mining areas; non-state armed groups
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit girls in rest stops, bars and restaurants along the Maputo–South Africa highway and around mines, and that non-state armed groups abducted children and sexually exploited girls. Girls as young as 11 working as nannies are vulnerable when employment ends.

n: South Africa — rural children trafficked to Gauteng and Western Cape (US TIP 2025)
who: Brothel owners and traffickers; some parents
cover: Low-level official corruption and complicity persisted.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit victims from rural areas, especially children, and exploit them in sex trafficking in cities, especially Gauteng and Western Cape; brothel owners use drugs to control victims including children; and some parents exploit their children in sex trafficking or online sexual exploitation for money or drugs.

n: Kamathipura, Mumbai — red-light district fed by trafficking from Nepal and Indian states
who: Brothels of Kamathipura
d: Kamathipura, Mumbai's oldest and largest red-light district and one of Asia's largest, was established over 150 years ago under British rule; the BBC in 2013 put its sex workers at an estimated 20,000. Girls were trafficked there from poor villages in other Indian states, some as young as 11, on promises of domestic work. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report is cited, though it could not be opened for this map, for a shift of sex trafficking in India toward spas, hotels and private residences, and for 2022 crime-data figures of 204 convicted traffickers and 1,134 acquittals; that report could not be opened in this pass (state.gov blocked).

n: Vietnam and Laos → China — girls sold as brides (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers and marriage brokers
d: The 2025 US TIP reports say traffickers in Vietnamese border villages lure women and girls, particularly Hmong, to China for forced marriages involving sex trafficking or forced labour, and use 'bride kidnapping' to exploit ethnic-minority girls in the northwest highlands; in Laos, traffickers increasingly kidnap or recruit women and girls via marriage brokers to China for sex trafficking, forced labour and forced surrogacy. Vietnam identified 236 child victims in 2024.

n: David Timothy Deakin — life sentence, Angeles City court (2020)
who: David Timothy Deakin (US national)
d: Acting on an FBI referral, the Philippine National Bureau of Investigation arrested US national David Timothy Deakin in Mabalacat, Pampanga, in 2017, rescuing two girls and seizing hard drives of abuse material; IJM said he abused Filipino children, recorded it and sold it online to foreign customers. In May 2020 the Angeles City Regional Trial Court Branch 58 convicted him of large-scale human trafficking and sentenced him to life imprisonment, in the country's first conviction delivered by videoconference. The 2025 US TIP report names Angeles City among tourist destinations with high demand for commercial sex.

n: South Korea — runaway children in commercial sex; police officer convicted (US TIP 2025)
who: Entertainment establishments, escort services, chat-room operators
cover: NGOs previously reported some local police sexually exploited children; one officer was convicted (bribery, secrecy violations) and another acquitted.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit South Korean women and children, including runaways, in bars, nightclubs and internet-advertised escort services, and chat-room operators coerce children with compromising images into producing sexual material. A court convicted a local police officer in a 2022 case involving alleged complicity in trafficking-related crimes and sentenced him to five years; another officer was acquitted.

n: Medellín — US federal prosecutions of travelling offenders (10 convictions by May 2026)
who: US-national travelling offenders; HSI Colombia; Alcaldía de Medellín
d: BluRadio reported on 21 May 2026 that US courts, working with Colombian authorities and the Medellín mayor's office, had handed down a tenth sentence in an offensive against foreigners exploiting children in Medellín: Ramón Arellano Sandoval, 65, sentenced in Miami to 30 years for attempted sexual exploitation of a 14-year-old Medellín girl, who had entered the city 48 times in two years. On 22 January 2026 Manuel Poceiro, 69, of Miami, was sentenced to life for travelling to Colombia to exploit minors, after HSI found material involving at least five minors. In March 2024 US national Timothy Alan Livingston was found in a Medellín hotel with two minors (aged between 12 and 16, per police sources); a Colombian judge issued an arrest warrant and Interpol a blue notice (charged, at large at the time).

n: La Pampa, Madre de Dios — Operación Mercurio 2019 and sex trafficking in mining camps
who: Bar/brothel networks serving illegal gold-mining camps
d: On 19–20 February 2019 more than 1,500 military and police began Operación Mercurio against illegal gold mining in La Pampa, in the Tambopata reserve buffer zone, under a state of emergency. Peru's Women's Minister said the worst crimes, including child sexual exploitation and child labour, had been committed there, and her ministry took in minors and women rescued from trafficking. Reporting in 2022 said police were still dismantling networks recruiting women to La Pampa bars; a 16-year-old girl previously rescued from a La Pampa trafficking band was found murdered at km 108 in April 2021.

n: Bolivia — foreign offenders in Indigenous communities near Rurrenabaque (US TIP 2025)
who: Foreign offenders; parents; online abuse-material producers
d: The 2025 US TIP report says foreign offenders exploited children in rural Indigenous communities in northern La Paz department, in and around Rurrenabaque and Santa Cruz, and in tourist areas of La Paz and Beni; production of abuse material for sale online is rising in Cochabamba, El Alto and Santa Cruz; and Bolivian women and girls are exploited in Argentina, Brazil, Chile, Panama and Peru. Tren de Aragua is reported to be involved in trafficking in Bolivia.

n: Costa Rica — child sex trafficking on Pacific coast and borders (US TIP 2025)
who: Traffickers in coastal tourist zones
d: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers subject Costa Rican women and children to sex trafficking, especially in Pacific coastal zones and near the northern and southern borders, where social tolerance increases children's vulnerability; girls from Nicaragua, Panama, the Dominican Republic and Venezuela are also identified as victims.

n: Galați/Brăila — 'loverboy' ring exploiting minors in Western Europe (2021)
who: Four suspects detained by DIICOT/BCCO
d: In February 2021 Romanian organised-crime police and DIICOT prosecutors searched eight addresses in Galați and Brăila and detained four suspects for human trafficking, trafficking of minors and pimping. Investigators said that from August 2013 the group recruited girls and young women by the 'loverboy' method, hid minors in intermediate lodgings until they turned 18, then exploited them in Western Europe, earning about €350,000; nine victims, minor and adult, had been identified.

n: Ukraine — wartime risk to evacuated institutional children; officials allegedly complicit (US TIP 2025)
who: Criminal networks; some institution officials
cover: Officials of several state-run residential institutions were allegedly complicit or negligent in trafficking of children in their care; no complicit officials convicted for the eighth year running.
d: The 2025 US TIP report says child sex trafficking in Ukraine is underreported and criminals are trying to build online networks to exploit Ukrainian children internationally; children evacuated from at least 195 facilities, including those with disabilities, are at high risk; and Ukrainian refugee women and children are vulnerable in Germany, France, Italy, Spain, Bulgaria and the UK. Ukraine convicted 24 traffickers in 2024, only six with prison terms.

n: Germany, Spain, Italy, Greece — romance-method pimps, Nigerian networks, unaccompanied children (US TIP 2025)
who: 'Loverboy' traffickers; Nigerian cult-linked groups; Eastern European recruiters
d: The 2025 US TIP reports say young male traffickers in Germany and Spain coerce girls into sex trafficking through sham romantic relationships; highly organized groups sometimes linked to Nigerian cult organizations exploit Nigerian women and girls in Germany and Italy, in Italy through debt and 'voodoo' rituals; Eastern European girls are recruited online for child sex trafficking in Italy; and in Greece unaccompanied children are vulnerable to sex trafficking and Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg.

n: US Angel Watch Center — 10,000+ notifications to foreign countries on travelling sex offenders
who: US Homeland Security Investigations; CBP; US Marshals Service
d: Under International Megan's Law (signed 2016), the Angel Watch Center notifies foreign governments when US registered child sex offenders plan to travel. DHS says that since 2016 it has made more than 10,000 notifications to foreign countries and notified the State Department of more than 3,500 passports carrying a sex-offender endorsement. HSI child-exploitation arrests rose to 3,771 in 2019 (ABC7, at the centre's ribbon-cutting).

n: Fr Joseph Jeyapaul — Indian priest extradited to Minnesota
who: Diocese of Crookston, Minnesota; diocese in India
cover: The Vatican recommended his removal from the priesthood, but the Indian bishop instead imposed a year in a monastery through a canonical trial, and he continued as a priest in India.
d: An Indian priest serving in the Diocese of Crookston in 2004–2005 was removed from ministry in September 2005 and returned to India. He was charged in 2006 with raping a girl from age 14; extradition took about five years after an Interpol alert, with arrest in Erode, India in 2012 and return to Minnesota in November 2014. In 2015 he pleaded guilty to criminal sexual misconduct involving a teenage girl and was sentenced to a year and a day (time served); the rape charges were dismissed under the plea deal and he faced deportation to India.

n: Paraguay — Fr Carlos Urrutigoity and the removal of Bishop Livieres
who: Diocese of Ciudad del Este
cover: After accusations in the US (a 2002 complaint over students at St Gregory's Academy in the Diocese of Scranton), he moved with his group to Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres in 2014; Urrutigoity left in June 2015. La Nación reported at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.
d: Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity was accused in 2002 in the US of sleeping with boarding-school students, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, and became its second-in-command in 2014. His case reportedly cost Bishop Livieres his post when Pope Francis removed him in 2014. He was moved back to Mendoza, Argentina, in June 2015. He has not been convicted.

n: IICSA — Child protection in religious organisations and settings (2021)
who: 38 religious organisations in England and Wales, including churches, mosques, synagogues, temples and out-of-school faith settings
cover: The Inquiry found victim-blaming, discouraging external reporting and putting reputation above victims; some organisations serving large congregations had no child protection policy at all.
d: The Independent Inquiry into Child Sexual Abuse published its report on 2 September 2021 after taking evidence from 38 religious organisations. It found child sexual abuse in most major UK religions and 'shocking failings' in prevention and response. An estimated 250,000 children attend faith-based supplementary or out-of-school settings, which need not register with any state body and have no child-protection oversight. Among cases heard, a mosque Qur'an teacher who abused four children aged about nine was convicted in 2017 and jailed for 13 years. It recommended that every religious organisation have a child protection policy and that the law on full-time education be changed so unregistered schools come under Ofsted.

n: Royal Commission Case Study 42 — Anglican Diocese of Newcastle
who: Anglican Diocese of Newcastle (Bishops Alfred Holland 1978–92, Roger Herft 1993–2005)
cover: Found a 'do nothing' approach under Bishop Holland and a 'weak and ineffectual' response under Bishop Herft; complainants were treated as liars and sometimes threatened with legal action; abusive relationships were misrepresented as consensual; dioceses receiving moved clergy were not warned; diocesan lawyers acted for accused priests. Former dean Graeme Lawrence was defrocked.
d: The Royal Commission's report, released on 7 December 2017 after hearings in August and November 2016, found systemic issues let a group of perpetrators operate in the diocese for at least 30 years. Fr Peter Rushton died in 2007 never charged, though the diocese acknowledges he was a child sex offender. Fr James Brown pleaded guilty in 2011 to 27 child sexual abuse charges relating to 19 boys and was jailed for up to 20 years. Bishop Herft resigned as Archbishop of Perth in 2016. Later bishops Brian Farran and Greg Thompson acted against alleged perpetrators and faced backlash.

n: Mexico — bishops say 152 priests removed in nine years
who: Mexican Episcopal Conference (CEM)
cover: The CEM president said there was no national count of victims because 'each bishop handles these problems' and no central record exists.
d: On 10 February 2019 Archbishop Rogelio Cabrera of Monterrey, president of the Mexican Episcopal Conference, said 152 priests had been removed from ministry in the previous nine years after being found guilty of sexually abusing minors, some of whom were jailed. He said there was no exact figure for victims.

n: Romania — former Bishop of Huși jailed for raping a seminary pupil
place: Huși, Vaslui County (St John Chrysostom Orthodox Theological Seminary)
who: Romanian Orthodox Church, Diocese of Huși; Huși Orthodox Theological Seminary
cover: The case surfaced in June 2017 when the bishop himself complained to anti-corruption prosecutors that three priests were blackmailing him with a recording; a former archimandrite was earlier jailed for that blackmail.
d: Romania's High Court of Cassation and Justice upheld a Galați Court of Appeal ruling sentencing former Bishop Corneliu Bârlădeanu (Cornel Onilă) to eight years for rape and other sexual assaults, in a case that began with 2017 recordings allegedly showing him with a minor pupil of the Huși seminary. Former archimandrite Sebastian Jitaru received 14 years 2 months for rape and sexual assaults. The diocese and seminary were ordered to pay court costs; the diocese apologised to the victims. Bârlădeanu resigned in August 2017. Media described him as the first senior Romanian Orthodox hierarch to go to prison.

n: Cloyne Report — Diocese of Cloyne
who: Catholic Diocese of Cloyne; Bishop John Magee
cover: Nine complaints that should have gone to the Gardaí were not reported; none of the 1996–2008 complaints reported to the health service; Vatican's reaction to Irish guidelines described as 'entirely unhelpful'
d: The Cloyne Report, published 13 July 2011, examined the diocese's handling of allegations against 19 clerics from 1996 to February 2009, after the Irish church had adopted reporting procedures. Nine complaints that should have been reported to the Gardaí were not, and none were reported to the health authorities. Bishop John Magee was found to have shown little interest in applying the guidelines for 12 years. The report said the Vatican's response to the Irish procedures allowed bishops to ignore them.

n: Pennsylvania grand jury — six dioceses
place: Pittsburgh, Harrisburg, Allentown, Scranton, Greensburg, Erie
who: Six Pennsylvania Catholic dioceses
cover: Abusers moved and protected, some later promoted; reports brushed aside; most crimes beyond statute of limitations
d: A 23-member statewide grand jury report released by Attorney General Josh Shapiro on 14 August 2018 identified 301 'predator priests' and at least 1,000 child victims over about 70 years in six dioceses. The roughly 1,400-page report found bishops 'went to great lengths to keep it secret' and moved abusers. Most crimes were too old to prosecute.

n: Missouri Attorney General — four Catholic dioceses
who: Archdiocese of St. Louis and dioceses of Kansas City–St. Joseph, Jefferson City, Springfield–Cape Girardeau
d: Attorney General Eric Schmitt reported on 13 September 2019 on a review, opened in August 2018, of records of more than 2,000 priests who served in Missouri since 1945. It found 163 credible allegations of abuse or misconduct against minors by diocesan priests and deacons; 83 of the accused had died and the statute of limitations had expired for 46 alleged crimes. Twelve former priests were referred for prosecution.

n: Royal Commission — Catholic Church data, Australia
who: Catholic Church in Australia, incl. St John of God Brothers (40.4% of brothers accused)
d: Data presented to the Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse on 6 February 2017 showed 4,444 people reported abuse to Catholic authorities between 1980 and 2015, at more than 1,000 institutions, naming 1,880 alleged perpetrators. About 7% of priests who served between 1950 and 2010 were alleged perpetrators; 40.4% of St John of God Brothers were accused. Religious brothers (32%) and priests (30%) were the largest groups. The commission referred 309 cases to police.

n: IICSA — Ampleforth and Downside Benedictine schools
who: English Benedictine Congregation — Ampleforth Abbey and Downside Abbey schools
cover: Both institutions for decades avoided giving police and social services information; 'tell them nothing' approach after 2001
d: The IICSA report of 9 August 2018 found a culture of acceptance of abuse at Ampleforth and Downside, where children as young as seven and eleven were abused over about four decades. Ten people linked to the schools, mostly monks, were convicted or cautioned for sexual or indecent-image offences. Both abbeys tried for decades to avoid passing information to police and social services.

n: MHG study — German Bishops' Conference
who: German Catholic dioceses
cover: Researchers found personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated
d: The study by researchers from Mannheim, Heidelberg and Giessen, commissioned by the German Bishops' Conference and presented on 25 September 2018, found 1,670 clerics (4.4% of clergy) accused of abusing 3,677 minors between 1946 and 2014. The authors called the figures conservative and found that personnel files had been destroyed or manipulated.

n: Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and Jesuit schools
who: Society of Jesus (Jesuits), Canisius-Kolleg Berlin and St. Blasien
cover: Superiors helped one admitted abuser, Fr Wolfgang S., emigrate to South America; offences time-barred
d: In January 2010 Fr Klaus Mertes, rector of the Jesuit Canisius-Kolleg in Berlin, wrote to about 600 former pupils who attended between 1975 and 1989, apologising for 'systematic assaults' by two priests who had taught there and asking other victims to come forward; he said there had been 'a culture of looking away'. The revelations opened the German church abuse scandal. Legal action was unlikely because of time limits. One of the former teachers, Wolfgang S., then living in South America, admitted he had abused children and young people for years and said he had told his Jesuit superiors in 1991.

n: Spanish Ombudsman report on Church abuse
who: Catholic Church in Spain
d: Spain's first official inquiry into clergy abuse, a nearly 800-page report by Ombudsman Ángel Gabilondo presented to parliament on 27 October 2023 after an 18-month investigation of 487 cases, criticised the church's response as often minimising or denying the problem. A GAD3 survey of 8,000 adults in the report found 1.13% said they had been abused as children by clergy or lay church members and 0.6% by clergy. Gabilondo did not extrapolate a victim count; media applying the percentages to Spain's adult population put the figure at about 440,000 (or about 200,000 for clergy alone). The Spanish bishops apologised but disputed the media figures.

n: Antonio Provolo Institute for the Deaf, Verona
who: Compagnia di Maria per l'educazione dei sordomuti (Provolo Institute); Diocese of Verona
cover: Fr Nicola Corradi, accused in Verona in 2009 and flagged by the diocese in 2011, was working at the institute's branch in Argentina, where he went on to abuse children
d: In 2009 former students of the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona went public: 67 people said they had been abused by 24 priests, lay people and religious brothers, and named Fr Nicola Corradi as being in Argentina. In 2012 the Diocese of Verona asked victims for forgiveness and sanctioned accused members, but Corradi was not among them and was never charged in Italy. He kept working at the Provolo school in Argentina, where he was arrested in 2016 and convicted in 2019.

n: Sodalicio de Vida Cristiana — suppressed by the Vatican 2025
who: Sodalitium Christianae Vitae; founder Luis Fernando Figari
cover: Abuse reported by journalists in 2015 after years of internal silence; journalists faced legal action; Vatican commission in 2023 led to mass expulsions
d: Journalists Pedro Salinas and Paola Ugaz exposed abuse by founder Luis Fernando Figari and associates in the 2015 book 'Mitad monjes, mitad soldados'. An apostolic visitor was appointed in 2015. In February 2017 the group gave Peruvian prosecutors information from an expert report on sexual abuse of minors by Figari and four former members, and the Vatican barred Figari from contact with members. After an investigation by Archbishop Charles Scicluna and Mgr Jordi Bertomeu, the Vatican expelled Figari in August 2024 over physical, psychological and sexual violence, including against minors. The society was formally suppressed by a decree signed on 14 April 2025.

n: Crimen sollicitationis — secrecy instruction (1962)
who: Holy See — Holy Office (now Dicastery for the Doctrine of the Faith)
cover: Church proceedings to be kept absolutely confidential under automatic excommunication, binding tribunal members, accusers and witnesses
d: The Holy Office instruction Crimen sollicitationis, approved by Pope John XXIII on 16 March 1962 and restating a 1922 instruction, governed canonical cases of solicitation in confession and also obscene acts with pre-adolescent children. It required absolute secrecy under pain of automatic excommunication. Many bishops did not know it was in their archives until press reports in 2003. Canon lawyer Thomas Doyle called the secrecy rules 'an explicit written policy to cover up cases', while others argue it did not bar reporting to police. It stayed in force until 2001.

n: Vos estis lux mundi (2019) and February 2019 summit
who: Pope Francis
d: Three months after a February 2019 Vatican summit of bishops' conference presidents on abuse, Pope Francis issued Vos estis lux mundi, published on 9 May 2019. It requires clerics and religious to report suspected abuse and cover-ups promptly to church authorities, requires every diocese to set up a public reporting system, and lets bishops be investigated for abuse or cover-up. It applies 'without prejudice' to state reporting laws but does not itself require reporting to civil authorities. A revised permanent version was decreed on 25 March 2023 and took effect on 30 April 2023.

n: Vatican tribunal — diplomat Carlo Capella and the Martinelli trial
who: Holy See diplomat Mgr Carlo Capella; St Pius X pre-seminary
d: On 23 June 2018 the Vatican tribunal convicted Mgr Carlo Capella, recalled in 2017 from the Holy See's embassy in Washington, of possessing and sharing child abuse images and sentenced him to five years. In October 2020 the first Vatican criminal trial for sexual abuse began: Fr Gabriele Martinelli was accused of abusing an altar boy at the St Pius X pre-seminary inside the Vatican, and former rector Enrico Radice was charged with aiding and abetting.

n: Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry — Sisters of Nazareth
who: Poor Sisters of Nazareth
d: The Scottish Child Abuse Inquiry found in May 2019 that children in Nazareth House orphanages from 1933 to 1984 suffered sexual abuse 'of the utmost depravity'. Police received more than 300 complaints. In 2025 the Sisters agreed to pay up to £5.75 million to survivors and three former staff were convicted.

n: Fr Paul Moore — moved by his bishop to Toronto
who: Diocese of Galloway; Bishop Maurice Taylor
cover: Bishop Maurice Taylor sent Moore to Toronto and Fort Augustus
d: Fr Francis 'Paul' Moore was found guilty at the High Court in Glasgow in 2018 of abusing three boys in Ayrshire in the 1970s and indecently assaulting a student priest in 1995, and was jailed for nine years. He had confessed his attraction to boys to Bishop Maurice Taylor of Galloway in 1996; Taylor sent him to a treatment centre in Toronto and to Fort Augustus Abbey, removed him from ministry but let him live in a church-bought house, and did not report him.

n: Archdiocese of Los Angeles — settlements 2007 and 2024
who: Roman Catholic Archdiocese of Los Angeles; Cardinal Roger Mahony
cover: In 2013 Archbishop Gómez removed Cardinal Mahony from public duties over his handling of abusive clergy
d: In July 2007 the Archdiocese of Los Angeles agreed a $660 million settlement with more than 500 people who said they were abused by more than 220 priests, teachers and other church employees, and Cardinal Roger Mahony apologised. In October 2024 it agreed to pay $880 million to 1,353 people, which experts called the largest single child sex abuse settlement with a Catholic archdiocese; total payouts reached more than $1.5 billion. In February 2013 Archbishop José Gómez barred Mahony from public ministry over his handling of abusers.

n: Christian Brothers in Australia — Ballarat and WA orphanages
place: Ballarat (St Alipius, St Patrick's); Bindoon, Clontarf, Castledare, Tardun (WA)
who: Congregation of Christian Brothers
cover: Convicted Brothers Dowlan and Best were moved from junior to senior campus and continued offending; leaders knew of abuse at WA orphanages for decades
d: Data presented to the Royal Commission in February 2017 showed that 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations. The order made the most compensation payments of any Catholic authority: 763, totalling A$48.5 million. In Ballarat, former Brothers Edward Dowlan and Robert Best, the principal of St Alipius school, were jailed for sexual crimes against pupils.

n: Marist Brothers and priests — New Zealand convictions
who: Marist Brothers; Society of Mary
d: A 2018 Otago Daily Times report listed nine Marist Brothers convicted of crimes against boys in New Zealand, including two at Hato Paora College. Marist priest Alan Woodcock was extradited from England and convicted in 2004 of 21 offences (1978–1987). Brother Kevin Healy was convicted in 2020. The church admitted in 2022 that 14% of its diocesan clergy had been accused since 1950.

n: St Michael's School, Soni — Rosminian priests
who: Institute of Charity (Rosminians); English priest Kit Cunningham and three others
cover: The order knew of Cunningham's abuse before his death in 2010; it became public only through a BBC documentary in June 2011
d: In the 1960s four Rosminian priests, including English priest Kit Cunningham, physically and sexually abused boys at St Michael's boarding school in Soni, Tanganyika (now Tanzania). The order openly acknowledged the crimes of the four priests but in 2010 refused to pay compensation; Cunningham died in December 2010. The abuse became public in the BBC documentary 'Abused: Breaking the Silence', broadcast on 21 June 2011. A group of 22 former Soni pupils pursued a compensation claim, and former pupils of Soni and the order's Grace Dieu school in Leicestershire announced they would sue.

n: Malta — St Joseph Home convictions
who: Missionary Society of St Paul (St Joseph Home); Maltese clergy
d: By April 2010 the church in Malta had recorded 84 allegations. Fr Charles Pulis was sentenced to six years and Fr Godwin Scerri to five years for abusing boys at a church children's home; Donald Bellizzi received three years in 2020.

n: Denis Chrysostom Alexander — extradition from Australia
who: Benedictine monk, Fort Augustus Abbey School
cover: Sent back to Australia by the school after parents complained; police not informed
d: Benedictine monk Denis 'Chrysostom' Alexander abused pupils at Fort Augustus Abbey School in Scotland in the 1970s. A 2013 BBC investigation reported that after a pupil told his parents, who complained to the school, Alexander was sent back to Australia with no warning about his offending; he became a parish priest in Sydney. Scotland requested his extradition in August 2016 and he was arrested in Sydney in January 2017. After contesting extradition he was returned to Scotland in January 2020. In June 2021 at the High Court in Edinburgh he pleaded guilty to indecent behaviour against two boys aged 12 to 14 between 1973 and 1976, and on 30 July 2021 he was jailed for four years and five months.

n: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
place: Iwerne camps (Dorset) and Winchester College; later Zambesi Ministries camps, Zimbabwe; Cape Town
who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cover: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.
d: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.

n: Southern Baptist Convention — Guidepost report and secret list of accused ministers
who: Southern Baptist Convention Executive Committee
cover: Former Executive Committee officials D. August Boto and Roger Oldham kept a private list of abusive ministers, but no one acted to keep them out of SBC pulpits; survivors met 'resistance, stonewalling, and even outright hostility' and were told church autonomy prevented action; a few senior leaders and outside counsel focused on avoiding liability.
d: Guidepost Solutions, hired after SBC delegates demanded an outside probe in 2021, released its report on 22 May 2022. It found a few senior Executive Committee leaders had for about two decades controlled the response to abuse reports to limit legal liability, ignoring or disbelieving survivors. The Executive Committee then published the previously secret list, 205 pages and 703 entries, on 26 May 2022.

n: Conti v. Watchtower — Fremont congregation, California
who: Watchtower Bible and Tract Society (Jehovah's Witnesses)
d: In June 2012 an Alameda County jury found the Watchtower Society liable for abuse of a girl by a congregation member and awarded punitive damages, later reduced. In April 2015 the California appeals court reversed punitive damages but upheld $2.8 million in compensatory damages; the case settled during further appeal. Other US civil cases followed, including a $13.5 million San Diego judgment in 2014 (vacated 2016, settled 2018) and a $35 million Montana verdict in 2018 reversed in 2020.

n: Malka Leifer — Adass Israel School, Melbourne
who: Adass Israel School (ultra-Orthodox community school)
cover: In March 2008, after a teacher confronted her, the school arranged and paid for a 1:20 a.m. flight to Israel for Leifer and four of her children without telling police. In Israel, then deputy health minister Yaakov Litzman pressured ministry staff to alter psychiatric evaluations so she would appear unfit for extradition; her lawyers sought more than 70 hearings and appeals.
d: Headmistress Malka Leifer abused pupils at Melbourne's ultra-Orthodox Adass Israel School between about 2003 and 2007. The school flew her to Israel in March 2008. Australia issued a warrant in 2014 for 74 offences involving at least eight pupils; she was arrested in Israel in August 2014, found in 2019 to have faked mental illness, and extradited on 25 January 2021. On 3 April 2023 a Melbourne jury found her guilty of 18 charges including rape, and in August 2023 she was sentenced to 15 years. In 2015 the Supreme Court of Victoria had ordered the school and Leifer to pay a former pupil about AU$1.27 million.

n: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
d: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.

n: Re ST (A Minor) — High Court judgment on The Family (Children of God)
who: The Family / Children of God (now The Family International)
d: In a custody case in the High Court Family Division, Lord Justice Alan Ward gave judgment in chambers on 26 May 1995 and handed it down publicly on 19 October 1995. He found that a high proportion of children in The Family were exposed to adult sexual activity and that a significant number had sexual activity forced on them by adults, and he described harsh discipline including silence restriction and exorcisms of children. He found the group had made changes he judged likely to be irreversible, let the mother keep custody on conditions, required the group to ban corporal punishment of children in the UK by anyone other than parents, and said it must denounce founder David Berg and acknowledge that through his writings he was personally responsible for children being subjected to sexually inappropriate behaviour.

n: Agape Boarding School — Christian boys' school, Missouri
who: Agape Boarding School (independent Baptist ministry)
cover: The state Attorney General's office said 22 workers should have been charged with serious crimes, but the county prosecutor charged five with low-level counts; in Missouri only the local prosecutor can file charges.
d: Former students came forward in 2020. In 2021 the school's longtime doctor, David Smock, was charged with child sex crimes and five staff with low-level abuse counts; two later pleaded guilty to misdemeanours. Missouri passed a 2021 law tightening oversight of religious boarding schools. Agape closed on 20 January 2023.

n: Manitoba Colony 'ghost rapes' — Mennonite colony, Bolivia
who: Old Colony Mennonite community, Manitoba Colony
cover: The attacks were first blamed on ghosts or demons; a 2013 investigation reported similar assaults continuing.
d: Men from the Manitoba Mennonite Colony sprayed a drug through bedroom windows to sedate households, then broke in and raped women and girls, including small children. The attacks came to light in June 2009. In August 2011 a Bolivian court convicted the men of raping and sexually assaulting 151 women and girls; seven were sentenced to 25 years and an eighth man got 12 years for supplying the drug.

n: Rev. Gordon Nakayama — Anglican dioceses of New Westminster and Calgary
place: Vancouver (Diocese of New Westminster) and Alberta (Diocese of Calgary)
who: Anglican Church of Canada; Japanese Canadian congregations
cover: Nakayama made a written confession in 1994; the dioceses did not report it to police. He was allowed to resign and died in 1995.
d: Gordon Goichi Nakayama served for more than 50 years as an Anglican priest to Japanese Canadian communities in the dioceses of Calgary and New Westminster. In 1994 he admitted a history of sexually abusing minors and shortly before his death in 1995 signed a written confession to Archbishop Barry Curtis; he was charged with immorality under church law and resigned from ministry, but police were not told. On 15 June 2015 the two dioceses formally apologised to survivors in Vancouver. The church said it is not known how many minors were abused.

n: Jesus Fellowship (Jesus Army) — Operation Lifeboat and redress scheme
who: Jesus Fellowship Church / Jesus Fellowship Community Trust
d: After founder Noel Stanton died in 2009, Northamptonshire Police ran Operation Lifeboat into historic abuse; about ten to twelve former members were convicted of sex offences. The church's redress scheme, whose final report was published on 11 September 2024, received 601 applications, paid £7.7 million, identified 539 alleged perpetrators and accepted responsibility for 264 of them, 61% of whom were former leaders.

n: Apollo Quiboloy — Kingdom of Jesus Christ
who: Kingdom of Jesus Christ (KOJC)
d: A federal grand jury in the Central District of California returned a 42-count superseding indictment on 10 November 2021 (unsealed 18 November) charging Quiboloy and eight church administrators, including with sex trafficking of children. It alleges females aged about 12 to 25 were recruited as personal assistants and required to have sex with him, and that church members were brought to the US on fraudulently obtained visas and forced to solicit donations for a sham charity. In 2024 the Philippine Department of Justice charged him with sexual abuse and a court ordered his arrest; after a two-week police operation at the church's Davao City compound he surrendered and was taken into custody on 8 September 2024. He denies the charges.

n: ISKCON boarding schools (gurukulas) — acknowledged abuse
place: ISKCON rural community boarding schools, US and India
who: International Society for Krishna Consciousness (ISKCON)
d: In the 1990s ISKCON leaders acknowledged physical, emotional and sexual abuse of children in the movement's boarding schools in the US and India in the 1970s and 1980s, and in 1998 ISKCON itself published an exposé. A $900 million lawsuit filed in Texas in 2002 (the Turley case) led ISKCON temples into Chapter 11 bankruptcy and a $15 million settlement in 2008. ISKCON then set up a Child Protection Office.

n: Devadasi dedication of girls — Karnataka and neighbouring states
who: Temple dedication practice (mostly Dalit girls)
d: Girls, mostly from Dalit families, are dedicated to temple deities and then sexually exploited, despite laws against the practice, including Karnataka's 1982 ban. The Karnataka government's last survey, in 2008, counted 40,600 devadasis; NGOs and a 2018 Karnataka State Women's University study found more than 80,000. Girls as young as seven have been pushed into the tradition.
